lessons.title: What Computer Graphics Is: Pixels, Raster and Vector Images
lessons.content:
Pick up your phone and look closely at the screen, really closely, maybe with a magnifying glass or the zoom of another phone's camera. The smooth photo of your family, the sharp letters of a WhatsApp message, the bright green field in a cricket game, all of it breaks down into a grid of tiny glowing squares. Every single one of those squares was told, by some program, exactly what colour to be, around 60 times every second. Computer graphics is the science of deciding those colours: how a computer turns ideas like a line, a circle, a 3D car or a sunset into millions of coloured dots, quickly and correctly.

What computer graphics is: Computer graphics is the part of computer science that deals with creating, storing, changing and displaying pictures using a computer. The input is usually a description: points, lines, shapes, 3D models, colours, lights and a camera. The output is an image on a screen, on paper or in a file. The opposite direction, taking a photo and understanding what is inside it, is called image processing or computer vision. Graphics goes from model to picture; vision goes from picture to model. This course is about the first direction.

Where graphics is used: Almost every screen you touch uses it. Games like PUBG Mobile or FIFA draw full 3D worlds in real time. Engineers use CAD (computer aided design) software to design buildings, bridges such as the Padma Bridge, and machine parts before anything is built. Google Maps and Barikoi draw roads and labels. Doctors look at 3D views of CT and MRI scans. Films and cartoons use graphics for effects and whole animated movies. Even the buttons, fonts and scroll animations of a simple app like bKash are drawn by graphics code. Data charts in a report, weather maps on TV and the Pathao rider moving on your map are graphics too.

A short history: In 1963 Ivan Sutherland built Sketchpad at MIT, a program where a user drew directly on a screen with a light pen and could move, copy and resize shapes. It is often called the start of interactive computer graphics. Early screens drew lines directly with an electron beam (vector displays). In the 1970s cheaper memory made raster displays with a frame buffer possible, and algorithms like Bresenham's line drawing, the z-buffer and Phong shading appeared. The 1980s and 1990s brought personal computers with graphical user interfaces, then 3D graphics cards. Today a phone contains a GPU, a graphics processing unit, that can shade billions of pixels per second.

The pixel: A raster screen is a rectangular grid of picture elements, called pixels. Each pixel shows one colour at a time. A pixel is addressed by two whole numbers, a column x and a row y. In many systems the origin (0,0) is at the top-left and y grows downwards, while in maths and in many graphics textbooks the origin is at the bottom-left and y grows upwards. Both are fine as long as you know which one you are using. A pixel is not a perfect little square of light in real hardware, but thinking of it as a small square cell is a good starting model.

Resolution: Resolution is the number of pixels across and down. Full HD is 1920 x 1080, which is 1920 times 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels, about 2 million. A 4K UHD screen is 3840 x 2160, which is exactly four times as many, about 8.3 million. More pixels can show finer detail, but they also need more memory and more work every frame. Pixel density, measured in pixels per inch (PPI), tells how tightly packed they are. A 6 inch phone with Full HD looks sharper than a 40 inch TV with the same resolution because its pixels are much smaller.

Raster images: A raster image, also called a bitmap, stores the colour of every pixel in a grid. A photo from your phone camera saved as JPEG or PNG is a raster image. Raster images are great for photos and complex scenes because any pattern of colours can be stored. Their weakness is scaling. If you zoom a small raster image a lot, each stored pixel becomes a big visible block, and edges look jagged or blurry. The image simply does not contain information finer than its pixels.

Vector images: A vector image stores shapes as mathematical descriptions instead of pixels. A circle is stored as centre (50, 50) and radius 20, with a red fill. A line is stored as its two end points and a thickness. When the image is shown, the program turns these descriptions into pixels at whatever size is needed. That is why logos, fonts and maps are usually vector: an SVG logo or a TrueType letter stays perfectly sharp whether printed on a visiting card or on a giant billboard at Kawran Bazar. The weakness is that a real photo with millions of different colours is very hard to describe as shapes.

Raster vs vector in one small example: Suppose you want a black circle of radius 100 on a 300 x 300 white canvas. As a raster PNG with 1 byte per pixel, you store 300 x 300 = 90,000 values (compression makes the file smaller, but the idea is a full grid). As a vector, you store roughly: circle, centre (150,150), radius 100, colour black, a few dozen bytes. If you now want the same picture at 3000 x 3000, the raster version must be redrawn or it will look blocky, while the vector version just gets drawn again at the larger size with smooth edges.

Rasterization, the central job: Since our screens are raster grids, every vector description must finally be converted into pixels. This conversion is called scan conversion or rasterization. Deciding which pixels best approximate a straight line from (2,3) to (10,8), which pixels lie on a circle, or which pixels are inside a triangle, are exactly the algorithms we study in the first part of this course: DDA, Bresenham, midpoint circle and ellipse, and polygon filling.

Object space and image space: Graphics people often say an algorithm works in object space or in image space. Object space means working with the geometric description itself, for example comparing two triangles in 3D to see which is in front. Image space means working pixel by pixel on the screen, for example storing a depth value for every pixel. We will meet this distinction again in hidden surface removal, where the z-buffer is an image space method and back-face culling works in object space.

Interactive and non-interactive graphics: In passive or non-interactive graphics the user only watches, like a printed chart or a pre-rendered movie. In interactive graphics the user changes the picture while it is shown: moving a game character, rotating a 3D model, zooming a map. Interactive graphics must be fast, usually 30 or 60 frames per second or more, so a lot of graphics research is about doing the same job with fewer calculations, which is why integer tricks like Bresenham's algorithm matter.

The basic pipeline in one paragraph: A typical 3D picture is made in steps. First we describe objects, usually as many small triangles. Then we place them in a world using transformations: move, rotate, scale. Then we choose a camera and project the 3D world onto a 2D image plane. We clip away parts outside the view. We decide which surfaces are hidden behind others. We compute colour using lights and materials. Finally we rasterize triangles into pixels and write them into a frame buffer that the display shows. Each of these steps is a lesson in this course.

The maths you need: You already know vectors, dot product, cross product and matrix multiplication from Linear Algebra, and you have seen 2D rotation and scaling matrices and homogeneous coordinates there. We will reuse them a lot, but always with graphics examples and small numbers. You also need simple coordinate geometry: the slope of a line, the equation of a circle, and similar triangles. No heavy calculus is required for this course.

Real life example 1, a Ludo game on your phone: When you roll the dice in a Ludo app, the board is probably stored as a raster image or drawn from vector shapes, the tokens are small images moved to new positions using translation, the dice spins using rotation, and everything is drawn into a frame buffer 60 times per second. If the tokens look slightly blurry when you zoom, that tells you they are raster images being scaled up.

Real life example 2, a shop banner at Dhaka New Market: A designer makes a banner in a tool like Illustrator or Inkscape using vector shapes and fonts, then sends it to a large-format printer. Because it is vector, the same file prints sharply at 1 metre or 10 metres wide. The printer itself is a raster device: it finally places tiny ink dots. So even here a vector description is rasterized at the last step.

The course map: We start with display hardware and the frame buffer. Then raster algorithms: lines with DDA and Bresenham, circles and ellipses with the midpoint method, polygon filling and antialiasing. Then 2D transformations with homogeneous matrices, windowing and viewports, and clipping with Cohen-Sutherland, Liang-Barsky and Sutherland-Hodgman. Then 3D: objects, transformations, projections and the viewing pipeline, followed by hidden surface removal. Then appearance: colour models, illumination, shading, curves and texture mapping. We finish with the modern GPU pipeline and shaders, animation basics and an introduction to ray tracing.

How to study this course: Draw. Keep graph paper and a pencil, and actually plot the pixels each algorithm picks. Run the decision parameters by hand in a small table; exams love these tables. When a formula appears, try it once with tiny numbers. If you can program, write each algorithm in a few lines of Python or C and print the pixel list; seeing your own code draw a circle is very satisfying.

Common mistakes: Thinking raster means bad quality and vector means good quality. Each is right for different jobs: photos are raster, logos are vector. Thinking a vector image is never turned into pixels. It always is, at display time. Mixing up computer graphics with image processing: graphics creates images from models, image processing changes or analyses existing images. And forgetting which way the y axis points on a given system, which flips pictures upside down.

What exams ask: Define computer graphics and list applications. Differentiate raster and vector graphics, or raster scan and random scan displays. Define pixel, resolution and aspect ratio, and compute pixel counts. Explain interactive versus passive graphics. Short notes on Sketchpad, rasterization or the graphics pipeline also appear.

Recap: Computer graphics turns descriptions of shapes, objects, lights and cameras into pictures. Screens are grids of pixels, described by resolution. Raster images store every pixel; vector images store shapes and are rasterized when shown. Rasterization, transformations, viewing, hidden surfaces and shading are the big steps of every rendering system, and this course walks through each of them. Next we look inside the display itself and the memory that holds the picture: the frame buffer.
key_points: Computer graphics creates and displays pictures from descriptions of shapes, objects, lights and cameras.
Image processing and computer vision go the other way: from images to information.
A raster screen is a grid of pixels; resolution is pixels across times pixels down (Full HD = 1920 x 1080, about 2.07 million).
Raster (bitmap) images store every pixel and are good for photos but get blocky when enlarged.
Vector images store shapes mathematically and stay sharp at any size, but are poor for photos.
Rasterization (scan conversion) turns shapes into pixels and is the core job of graphics.
Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad (1963) is often called the start of interactive computer graphics.
The course follows the pipeline: raster algorithms, 2D transforms and clipping, 3D viewing, hidden surfaces, colour and shading, GPU and ray tracing.
lessons.tip: Buy a cheap graph-paper notebook just for this course. Every algorithm from lesson 3 onwards, plot its pixels by hand at least once; your eyes will catch mistakes your calculations miss.

lessons.title: Display Hardware and the Frame Buffer
lessons.content:
Think of a big stadium card show, like the crowd pictures you see in opening ceremonies. Thousands of people each hold up a coloured card, and together they form a giant flag of Bangladesh. Each person is a pixel. But someone must have a master sheet that says which colour each seat should show, and the crowd must read it and hold up the right card, again and again. In a computer, that master sheet is a block of memory called the frame buffer, and the crowd is the display. This lesson is about how the picture in memory becomes light on the screen.

Why hardware matters for graphics: Every algorithm in this course ends by writing colours into memory. How much memory that takes, how fast it must be read, and why screens flicker or tear all depend on the display hardware. You do not need to be an electronics engineer, but you must know the vocabulary: raster scan, random scan, refresh rate, frame buffer, bit depth, lookup table, double buffering and aspect ratio. Exams ask these directly.

The CRT, the classic display: For decades screens were cathode ray tubes (CRTs). At the back sits an electron gun that shoots a narrow beam of electrons. Deflection coils or plates bend the beam left-right and up-down. Where the beam hits the front glass, a phosphor coating glows. In colour CRTs there are three guns and tiny red, green and blue phosphor dots for each spot. The glow fades quickly, in a fraction of a second; the time it keeps glowing is called persistence. So the picture must be redrawn many times per second, or it fades and flickers. Redrawing is called refreshing.

Refresh rate: The number of times per second the whole screen is redrawn is the refresh rate, measured in hertz. If it is too low, say below about 50 Hz, many people see flicker. Common values today are 60 Hz, and gaming monitors and many phones run at 90, 120 or 144 Hz. Do not confuse refresh rate with frame rate: refresh rate is how often the display shows a picture; frame rate is how often the program produces a new picture. A game running at 30 frames per second on a 60 Hz screen shows each frame twice.

Raster scan displays: In a raster scan system the beam sweeps the whole screen in a fixed pattern, row by row. It starts at the top-left, moves across the first row (a scan line), switching the beam stronger or weaker according to each pixel's value, then quickly jumps back to the left of the next row. That jump is the horizontal retrace. After the last row, the beam returns to the top-left; this is the vertical retrace. The picture comes from a frame buffer holding a value for every pixel. Television and almost all modern computer displays work in the raster way, which is why they can show photos and filled areas easily.

Interlacing: Older TVs used a trick to reduce flicker with limited bandwidth. Instead of drawing all lines in one pass, they drew the odd numbered lines in one pass (one field) and the even lines in the next pass. Two fields make one frame. The eye sees the screen refreshed twice as often, although each full frame still takes two passes. This is interlaced scanning, the i in 1080i; drawing all lines in order is progressive scanning, the p in 1080p.

Random scan (vector) displays: In a random scan display, also called vector or calligraphic display, the beam does not sweep every row. It moves directly from one point to another, drawing only the lines of the picture, like a pen plotter in light. The picture is stored as a list of line drawing commands called a display list or display file, and the system runs through this list 30 to 60 times per second. Lines look very smooth because there are no pixel steps. But filled areas and photos are almost impossible, and a very complex drawing with too many lines takes too long to refresh and begins to flicker. Early CAD systems and some radar screens used this approach.

Raster vs random scan in one table of words: Raster scan draws the whole screen every refresh, stores pixels in a frame buffer, handles filled areas, photos and colour well, but lines show jagged steps. Random scan draws only the lines, stores drawing commands, gives very smooth lines, and its refresh time depends on picture complexity. Exams often ask for exactly this comparison.

Flat panels: LCD, LED and OLED: Modern screens are flat panels. An LCD (liquid crystal display) has a light source behind it, the backlight, and in front of each subpixel a cell of liquid crystal between polarizing filters. A voltage changes how the crystals twist the light, so each cell lets more or less light through a red, green or blue filter. What shops call an LED TV is usually an LCD with an LED backlight. An OLED screen is different: each subpixel is an organic LED that makes its own light, so a black pixel is simply switched off, giving deep blacks and thin panels; many modern phones use OLED. Although none of these use an electron beam, they still update the image row by row from a frame buffer, so the raster ideas remain.

The frame buffer: The frame buffer, also called refresh buffer, is the memory that holds the colour value of every pixel. A part of the graphics hardware called the video controller (display controller) reads the frame buffer row by row, in step with the display's refresh, and sends the values to the screen. The program never draws on the glass directly; it only writes numbers into the frame buffer. Change the numbers and the next refresh shows the change.

Bit depth: How many bits are stored per pixel is the bit depth or colour depth. With 1 bit per pixel each pixel is either on or off, a black and white bitmap. With 8 bits there are 2^8 = 256 possible values. With 24 bits, 8 bits each for red, green and blue, there are 2^24 = 16,777,216 colours, called true colour. Often a fourth 8-bit channel called alpha is stored for transparency, making 32 bits per pixel.

Worked example, frame buffer size: How much memory does a 1920 x 1080 frame buffer need at 24 bits per pixel? Pixels = 1920 x 1080 = 2,073,600. Bytes per pixel = 24 / 8 = 3. Memory = 2,073,600 x 3 = 6,220,800 bytes. Dividing by 1,048,576 bytes per MiB gives about 5.93 MiB. At 60 refreshes per second the video controller must read 6,220,800 x 60 = 373,248,000 bytes per second, about 373 MB/s, just to show the picture. For a smaller example, 640 x 480 at 24 bits needs 640 x 480 x 3 = 921,600 bytes.

The colour lookup table: When memory was expensive, systems stored fewer bits per pixel and used a colour lookup table (CLUT), also called a palette. Each pixel stores an 8-bit index from 0 to 255. The table has 256 entries, and each entry holds a full 24-bit colour. To show a pixel, the controller reads its index, looks up the entry, and sends that colour. The image can use any 256 colours out of 16.7 million at once. A 640 x 480 image then needs 307,200 bytes plus a 768-byte table instead of 921,600 bytes. A neat trick: changing one table entry instantly changes every pixel using that index, which old games used for simple animation like flowing water. GIF images still use a palette of up to 256 colours.

Double buffering and tearing: If the program draws a new picture directly into the frame buffer that is being shown, the viewer may see half-drawn frames, and if the image changes while the controller is in the middle of the screen, the top part shows the old frame and the bottom part the new one, a visible horizontal break called tearing. The solution is double buffering: two buffers, a front buffer being displayed and a back buffer being drawn. When the new frame is complete, the two are swapped, ideally during the vertical retrace (vertical blank). Waiting for that moment is called vertical sync, or vsync. The cost is twice the memory.

Aspect ratio: Aspect ratio is the ratio of width to height. A 1920 x 1080 screen has 1920 / 1080 = 16 / 9, written 16:9; old monitors were 4:3, like 1024 x 768. There is also pixel aspect ratio: if pixels are not square, a mathematically perfect circle will look like an ellipse unless the program corrects for it. Most modern displays have square pixels, which makes our algorithms simpler.

Real life example 1, a phone screen: A phone with a 2400 x 1080 OLED panel at 32 bits per pixel needs 2400 x 1080 x 4 = 10,368,000 bytes, about 10 MB, per buffer. With double buffering that doubles. At 120 Hz the display pipeline reads the shown buffer 120 times a second. This is one reason a high refresh rate setting drains battery faster: more frames to produce and more data to move.

Real life example 2, a cricket match on an old TV: Grandfather's old CRT television in a village tea stall shows a Bangladesh match with a slight flicker and thin horizontal lines visible on fast moving players. That is interlacing at work: each field holds only half the lines, so fast motion between fields creates a comb-like edge. A modern LED TV showing the same match progressively looks steadier.

Common mistakes: Confusing refresh rate with frame rate. Thinking an LED TV is the same as an OLED TV. Forgetting to divide bits by 8 when computing bytes, or using 1,000,000 instead of 1,048,576 without saying which. Thinking random scan stores pixels; it stores line commands. And thinking a lookup table reduces the number of colours a screen can ever show; it limits how many can appear at once.

What exams ask: Compare raster and random scan displays. Explain the working of a CRT and the meaning of refresh, persistence and interlacing. Compute frame buffer size for a given resolution and bit depth. Explain the colour lookup table with an example. Explain double buffering and why it prevents flicker and tearing. Define aspect ratio.

Recap: Displays must be refreshed many times per second. Raster scan sweeps every row and shows the contents of a frame buffer; random scan draws only lines from a display list. Flat panels like LCD and OLED replaced CRTs but still update from a frame buffer. Memory = width x height x bits per pixel / 8. Lookup tables save memory, and double buffering hides drawing and prevents tearing. Next we start writing pixels into that frame buffer with our first algorithm: drawing a line.
key_points: A CRT shoots an electron beam at phosphor that glows briefly, so the picture must be refreshed many times per second.
Raster scan sweeps every row using horizontal and vertical retrace and shows a frame buffer; random scan draws only lines from a display list.
Interlacing draws odd lines then even lines (two fields per frame); progressive scanning draws all lines in order.
LCD panels filter a backlight; OLED subpixels emit their own light; both still refresh from a frame buffer.
Frame buffer memory = width x height x bits per pixel / 8; 1920 x 1080 x 24 bits = 6,220,800 bytes (about 5.93 MiB).
A colour lookup table stores small indices per pixel and a table of full colours, saving memory.
Double buffering draws into a back buffer and swaps during vertical blank to avoid flicker and tearing.
Aspect ratio is width to height, e.g. 16:9; non-square pixels distort circles.
lessons.tip: Memorise one worked frame buffer calculation with units written at every step (pixels, bits, bytes, MiB). Exams often give odd resolutions, and the units are where marks are lost.
lessons.task: Find your phone's screen resolution (Settings or a quick web search of the model). Compute its frame buffer size at 32 bits per pixel, then the bytes read per second at 60 Hz and at 120 Hz.

lessons.title: Drawing Lines: Output Primitives and the DDA Algorithm
lessons.content:
Imagine you are tiling a floor with square tiles, and someone asks you to make a straight diagonal line of black tiles from one corner of the room to a spot on the far wall. You cannot cut tiles; each tile is either black or white. So you walk along the wall, one tile at a time, and at each step you ask: which tile is closest to the true line? The line you get is a staircase, but a good staircase looks straight from a distance. A computer screen is exactly that floor of tiles, and drawing a line on it is the first real problem of raster graphics.

Output primitives: The simplest building blocks a graphics system can draw are called output primitives: points, straight line segments, circles and other curves, filled polygons and text. Everything else, from a bar chart to a building plan, is made of these. A point is easy: set one pixel in the frame buffer, often written setPixel(x, y, colour). A line is the first primitive that needs an algorithm, because we must choose many pixels that together look like a straight segment between two end points.

Pixel coordinates: In this lesson pixels sit at integer coordinates (x, y). A line from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) with integer end points passes between pixel centres most of the time, so at each step we must pick the nearest pixel. Our goal is three things: the line should look straight, it should look continuous with no gaps, and it should be drawn fast, because a game may draw millions of line pixels every second.

The line equation: From school geometry, a straight line can be written y = m x + b. The slope is m = dy / dx, where dx = x1 - x0 and dy = y1 - y0, and b is where the line crosses the y axis: b = y0 - m x0. For the line from (2,3) to (10,8): dx = 8, dy = 5, m = 5/8 = 0.625, and b = 3 - 0.625 x 2 = 1.75.

The naive method: Step x from x0 to x1 one pixel at a time, compute y = m x + b and round it. At x = 3, y = 0.625 x 3 + 1.75 = 3.625, rounded to 4. It works for gentle slopes, but every pixel needs a floating point multiplication and an addition, plus rounding. Worse, if the slope is steep, say m = 4, stepping x by 1 makes y jump by 4, leaving gaps in the line. We need something cheaper and gap-free.

The DDA idea: DDA stands for Digital Differential Analyzer. The key observation is that on a straight line, when x increases by 1, y always increases by exactly m. So instead of computing m x + b each time, we keep the previous y and add m. This turns a multiplication into an addition, an incremental method. In general, if x changes by delta x, y changes by m times delta x. DDA chooses the direction with more change and steps that one by exactly 1 per pixel.

Choosing the number of steps: Let steps = max(|dx|, |dy|). Then x increment = dx / steps and y increment = dy / steps. One of these increments is always +1 or -1, and the other has absolute value at most 1. That guarantees no gaps: in the direction of the larger change, we put exactly one pixel per column or per row.

The DDA algorithm in pseudo-code: dx = x1 - x0; dy = y1 - y0; steps = max(|dx|, |dy|); xinc = dx / steps; yinc = dy / steps; x = x0; y = y0; setPixel(round(x), round(y)); repeat steps times: x = x + xinc; y = y + yinc; setPixel(round(x), round(y)). That is all. Note that x and y are kept as real numbers; only the plotted pixel is rounded.

Worked example, (2,3) to (10,8): dx = 8, dy = 5, so steps = 8, xinc = 8/8 = 1, yinc = 5/8 = 0.625. Start at (2, 3) and plot (2, 3). Step 1: x = 3, y = 3.625, plot (3, 4). Step 2: x = 4, y = 4.25, plot (4, 4). Step 3: x = 5, y = 4.875, plot (5, 5). Step 4: x = 6, y = 5.5, plot (6, 6), rounding half up. Step 5: x = 7, y = 6.125, plot (7, 6). Step 6: x = 8, y = 6.75, plot (8, 7). Step 7: x = 9, y = 7.375, plot (9, 7). Step 8: x = 10, y = 8, plot (10, 8). The pixels are (2,3), (3,4), (4,4), (5,5), (6,6), (7,6), (8,7), (9,7), (10,8): nine pixels, one per column, ending exactly at the end point.

Worked example, a steep line (0,0) to (3,7): dx = 3, dy = 7, so steps = 7, xinc = 3/7, about 0.4286, yinc = 1. Now y moves by 1 each step and x creeps. The x values are 0.43, 0.86, 1.29, 1.71, 2.14, 2.57, 3.00, which round to 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3. Pixels: (0,0), (0,1), (1,2), (1,3), (2,4), (2,5), (3,6), (3,7). One pixel per row, no gaps. If we had wrongly stepped x by 1, we would plot only 4 pixels for a line 7 rows tall, with big holes.

Negative slopes and direction: DDA handles all directions automatically because the increments carry the sign. For (0,0) to (5,-3): steps = 5, xinc = 1, yinc = -0.6. The y values are -0.6, -1.2, -1.8, -2.4, -3.0, which round to -1, -1, -2, -2, -3. Pixels: (0,0), (1,-1), (2,-1), (3,-2), (4,-2), (5,-3). If the line is given from right to left, dx is negative and xinc becomes -1; the same pixels are drawn in reverse order.

Why DDA is better than the naive method: It removes the multiplication per pixel, replacing it with additions. It automatically avoids gaps by stepping along the major axis. It is simple to write and easy to understand, which is why it appears in every syllabus and every exam.

The weaknesses of DDA: First, it still uses floating point numbers and a rounding operation for every pixel. On older hardware, and even now in tight loops, integer operations are cheaper. Second, because yinc is stored with limited precision, adding it hundreds of times accumulates round-off error. For a very long line the computed position can drift away from the true line, and the last pixel might not match the end point exactly. Third, rounding itself costs time. These weaknesses are what Bresenham's algorithm, the next lesson, removes by using only integers.

A note on rounding: Different books round 0.5 differently. Rounding half up gives 5.5 to 6, as we did. Some languages round half to even (Python's round gives 6 for 5.5 but 4 for 4.5). In exams, say which rule you use and stay consistent. A common safe formula is floor(v + 0.5).

Line attributes in brief: Real systems also let you set line width, line style (solid, dashed, dotted) and colour. A dashed line can be drawn by the same DDA loop, turning setPixel on for some steps and off for others, like a pattern 11110000 repeated. A thick line can be drawn by plotting a short vertical span at each column for gentle slopes, or a horizontal span for steep ones. These ideas reappear when we discuss attributes and antialiasing.

Counting the work: For our first example, DDA did 8 additions for x, 8 additions for y and 16 rounding operations, and no multiplications at all. The naive method did 8 multiplications, 8 additions and 8 roundings for y alone. On a modern computer both finish in a blink, but a 4K game screen may draw tens of millions of edge pixels per second, and in the 1960s and 1970s plotters and display processors had very weak arithmetic. Saving one multiplication per pixel was a big deal, and saving the floating point entirely, as Bresenham does, was even bigger.

Why diagonal lines look dimmer: A horizontal line of 10 pixels covers a length of 10 units. A 45 degree line from (0,0) to (10,10) also uses 11 pixels, one per column, but its true length is about 14.1 units, because the length is 10 times the square root of 2. The same number of pixels is spread over a longer distance, so the diagonal line looks a little thinner and dimmer than the horizontal one. High quality systems correct this by adjusting intensity with the slope or by using antialiasing, which we will meet in lesson 8.

Polylines: Most drawings are not single lines but chains of connected segments, called polylines: the outline of a country on a map, a graph of temperature over a week, the edge of a polygon. A polyline with points P0, P1, P2, P3 is drawn by running the line algorithm on P0P1, then P1P2, then P2P3. One small care is needed: the shared end point, like P1, would be plotted twice. For a solid colour that is harmless, but for transparent drawing or XOR drawing it makes a visible dot, so careful code skips the first pixel of every segment after the first.

Real life example 1, a cricket wagon wheel: TV graphics during a Bangladesh match show a wagon wheel, lines from the batter to where each shot went. Each of those lines is drawn by a line algorithm from the crease point to the boundary point. Short lines need few steps, long ones many, and DDA would choose steps = max(|dx|, |dy|) for each.

Real life example 2, a ride route on a map: When a delivery app like Foodpanda draws your rider's path as a polyline, it is a series of straight segments between GPS points. Each segment is converted to pixels with a line algorithm. When you zoom in, the end points move and the lines are re-rasterized, which is why the route stays crisp at every zoom level.

Common mistakes: Always stepping x by 1, even for steep lines, which leaves gaps. Rounding x and y and then adding increments to the rounded values, which destroys accuracy; keep the real values and round only when plotting. Forgetting to plot the starting pixel, giving steps pixels instead of steps + 1. Forgetting the sign of the increments for lines going left or down.

What exams ask: State the DDA algorithm and trace it for given end points in a table of k, x, y and plotted pixel. Explain why steps = max(|dx|, |dy|). List advantages and disadvantages of DDA, and compare it with Bresenham. Sometimes they ask you to plot the pixels on a grid.

Recap: A line is drawn by picking, at each step along its longer direction, the pixel closest to the true line. DDA does this incrementally: it adds a constant increment to x and y each step and rounds for plotting. It avoids multiplication and gaps but uses floating point and accumulates round-off. Next lesson, Bresenham makes the same decisions using only integer additions and a sign test.
key_points: Output primitives are points, lines, curves, filled polygons and text.
A line y = m x + b has slope m = dy/dx; computing it per pixel needs a multiplication and leaves gaps for steep slopes.
DDA is incremental: each step adds a constant increment instead of recomputing the equation.
steps = max(|dx|, |dy|); xinc = dx/steps and yinc = dy/steps, so the major axis moves by exactly 1 per pixel.
Keep x and y as real numbers and round only when plotting.
DDA's drawbacks are floating point arithmetic, rounding cost and accumulated round-off error on long lines.
Line attributes like dashed or thick lines can be built on top of the same stepping loop.
lessons.tip: Always draw a table with columns k, x, y, round(x), round(y) when tracing DDA. Examiners give marks for the table even if one rounding slips.
lessons.task: On graph paper, trace DDA for the line from (1,1) to (6,9). Decide steps, the two increments, list all pixels, and colour them in. Check that the line has exactly one pixel per row.

quiz.q: In DDA, how is the number of steps chosen?
quiz.explain: Stepping along the larger change gives exactly one pixel per column or row and avoids gaps.

quiz.q: For the line (2,3) to (10,8), what is the y increment in DDA?
quiz.explain: steps = 8, so yinc = dy/steps = 5/8 = 0.625.

quiz.q: What is the main reason DDA is faster than computing y = m x + b at every pixel?
options: It replaces a multiplication with an addition per step
quiz.explain: DDA is incremental: it adds a constant instead of multiplying each time. It still uses floating point and rounding.

quiz.q: Which is a known weakness of DDA?
options: It leaves gaps on steep lines
Round-off error can accumulate on long lines
It only works for positive slopes
quiz.explain: Repeatedly adding a finite precision increment can drift on long lines.

quiz.q: For the line (0,0) to (3,7), which pixel does DDA plot at y = 3?
quiz.explain: xinc = 3/7; at y = 3, x = 9/7 = 1.29, which rounds to 1.

lessons.title: Bresenham's Line Algorithm: Lines with Integers Only
lessons.content:
Think of a rickshaw puller riding along a road with lane markings, trying to stay close to a straight chalk line drawn by a child on the road. At every metre he only asks one tiny question: should I stay in this lane or shift one lane up? He never measures exact distances with a ruler; he keeps a simple running score in his head of how far he is drifting, and when the score says he has drifted too far, he shifts. Bresenham's line algorithm is exactly that: at every pixel it asks a yes-or-no question using a running integer score, with no fractions, no multiplication and no rounding.

Why we needed something better than DDA: In the last lesson DDA drew lines by adding a fractional increment like 0.625 at every step and rounding. That needs floating point arithmetic, a rounding operation per pixel, and slowly accumulates error. In 1962 Jack Bresenham, working at IBM on controlling a digital pen plotter, published a method that makes the same pixel choices using only integer addition, subtraction and a sign test. It became the classic line algorithm for raster graphics, and the same incremental idea later gave us the midpoint circle and ellipse algorithms.

The setting: First we solve the simplest case: a line from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) with x0 < x1 and slope m between 0 and 1. In this case x is the major axis, so we step x by exactly 1 each time, like DDA. The only question at each step is about y: if the current pixel is (xk, yk), the next pixel is either (xk + 1, yk), going straight right, or (xk + 1, yk + 1), going diagonally up. Only two candidates. Our job is to choose the one closer to the true line.

Measuring the two distances: At x = xk + 1 the true line has y = m(xk + 1) + b. The distance from the lower candidate up to the line is d1 = y - yk. The distance from the line up to the upper candidate is d2 = (yk + 1) - y. If d1 < d2 the line is closer to the lower pixel; otherwise it is closer to the upper one. So we only need the sign of d1 - d2 = 2m(xk + 1) - 2yk + 2b - 1.

Getting rid of fractions: The slope m = dy/dx is a fraction. Multiply the whole expression by dx, which is positive, so the sign does not change. Define the decision parameter pk = dx (d1 - d2) = 2 dy xk - 2 dx yk + c, where c = 2 dy + dx (2b - 1) is a constant that does not depend on k. Now pk is an integer, and the rule is: if pk < 0, the lower pixel is closer, so choose yk + 1 = yk; otherwise choose yk + 1 = yk + 1. Here the subscript k+1 means the next step.

The incremental update: Computing pk from that formula every step would still be work. Instead subtract pk from the next value: p(k+1) - pk = 2 dy (x(k+1) - xk) - 2 dx (y(k+1) - yk). Since x always grows by 1, this becomes p(k+1) = pk + 2 dy - 2 dx (y(k+1) - yk). The last bracket is 0 if we stayed and 1 if we moved up. So: if pk < 0, p(k+1) = pk + 2 dy; if pk >= 0, p(k+1) = pk + 2 dy - 2 dx. Both 2 dy and 2 dy - 2 dx are computed once before the loop.

The starting value: Plugging the first point (x0, y0) into the formula and using b = y0 - m x0 gives a neat result: p0 = 2 dy - dx. You do not have to remember the derivation in the exam, but you must remember these three facts: p0 = 2dy - dx, add 2dy when p is negative, add 2dy - 2dx when p is zero or positive and step y up.

The algorithm in pseudo-code: dx = x1 - x0; dy = y1 - y0; p = 2*dy - dx; twoDy = 2*dy; twoDyDx = 2*(dy - dx); x = x0; y = y0; setPixel(x, y); while x < x1: x = x + 1; if p < 0: p = p + twoDy else: y = y + 1; p = p + twoDyDx; setPixel(x, y). Every operation inside the loop is an integer addition, an increment or a comparison with zero.

Worked example 1, (2,3) to (10,8): dx = 8, dy = 5, so p0 = 2 x 5 - 8 = 2, 2dy = 10 and 2dy - 2dx = 10 - 16 = -6. Plot (2,3). k = 0: p = 2, not negative, so y goes up: plot (3,4), new p = 2 - 6 = -4. k = 1: p = -4, negative, stay: plot (4,4), new p = -4 + 10 = 6. k = 2: p = 6, go up: plot (5,5), new p = 0. k = 3: p = 0, not negative, go up: plot (6,6), new p = -6. k = 4: p = -6, stay: plot (7,6), new p = 4. k = 5: p = 4, up: plot (8,7), new p = -2. k = 6: p = -2, stay: plot (9,7), new p = 8. k = 7: p = 8, up: plot (10,8). Done. Exactly the same nine pixels DDA gave us, but with integer additions only.

Worked example 2, the textbook line (20,10) to (30,18): dx = 10, dy = 8, so p0 = 16 - 10 = 6, 2dy = 16, 2dy - 2dx = -4. The decision values are 6, 2, -2, 14, 10, 6, 2, -2, 14, 10. The pixels after (20,10) are (21,11), (22,12), (23,12), (24,13), (25,14), (26,15), (27,16), (28,16), (29,17), (30,18). Notice the rhythm: two negative p values cause the two horizontal steps at x = 23 and x = 28; every other step goes diagonally. The pattern repeats because the slope 8/10 is a simple fraction.

How to read the decision parameter: pk is like the rickshaw puller's drift score. A negative score says the true line is still below the midpoint between the two candidates, so stay. A positive score says the line has climbed past the midpoint, so step up. Each step right adds 2dy to the score because the line rises by dy/dx per step (scaled by 2dx). Each step up subtracts 2dx because we caught up one full pixel (also scaled). The score never needs a fraction because everything was multiplied by 2dx at the start.

Two quick checks for your table: In the gentle case the line always has exactly dx + 1 pixels, one per column, and y must move up exactly dy times in total, because it has to climb from y0 to y1. In example 1 there are 9 pixels and five up-steps (at k = 0, 2, 3, 5, 7); in example 2 there are 11 pixels and eight up-steps. Also, the decision value always stays within a small band: it never grows without limit, because every time it becomes non-negative we subtract. If your p values keep growing, you have a sign mistake. These checks take ten seconds in an exam and catch most errors.

The midpoint view: Many books, including Hearn and Baker, also describe Bresenham as a midpoint algorithm. At each step, look at the midpoint between the two candidate pixels, (xk + 1, yk + 0.5). If the midpoint is below the line, the line passes closer to the upper pixel; if above, closer to the lower. Testing which side of the line a point lies on uses the implicit line function F(x, y) = dy x - dx y + c, which is zero on the line. Working through it gives the same integer decision parameter. This midpoint view is useful because the same thinking extends to circles and ellipses in the next two lessons.

Other slopes and directions: For slope between 0 and 1 going left to right we are done. For other cases we use symmetry. If the line goes right to left, swap the two end points. If the slope is negative, step y by -1 instead of +1 and use |dy|. If the slope is steeper than 1, swap the roles of x and y: y becomes the major axis and steps by 1 every time, and x is the one that decides whether to move, with p0 = 2|dx| - |dy|. Horizontal, vertical and exact 45 degree lines can be drawn directly without any decision at all, which real code often does for speed.

Why it was a big deal: Integer addition and sign tests were much cheaper than floating point on 1960s to 1980s hardware, and they still map nicely onto simple hardware circuits. There is no accumulated error: the decision parameter is exact, so the last pixel always lands exactly on the end point. Plotters, early display processors, printers and many software rasterizers used it. Even today, rasterizing thin lines and the edges of shapes in many 2D libraries relies on the same incremental integer idea.

Real life example 1, a digital signature pad: When a customer signs on a delivery app screen or a bKash agent's tablet, the touch screen reports a point every few milliseconds. The app joins consecutive points with short line segments. With hundreds of segments per second on a cheap phone, an integer line method keeps the drawing smooth without heating the processor.

Real life example 2, a laser cutter or CNC router in a Dhaka workshop: Stepper motors move the cutting head in fixed tiny steps along x and y, just like pixels. To cut a straight diagonal edge on a wooden sign, the controller must decide at each step whether to move x only or x and y together. That is literally Bresenham's problem, and motion controllers commonly use the same kind of incremental integer stepping.

Common mistakes: Using p0 = 2dx - dy for a gentle slope (that is for the steep case). Adding 2dy - 2dx when p is negative instead of positive. Updating p but forgetting to also increment y in the positive case. Treating p = 0 inconsistently: the usual rule is that p < 0 means stay and p >= 0 means move up; say this rule in your answer. Applying the gentle slope rules to a line with slope 2 and getting a gappy line.

What exams ask: Derive the Bresenham decision parameter for 0 < m < 1. Trace the algorithm for given end points in a table of k, pk, (xk+1, yk+1). Explain how it handles other slopes. Compare DDA and Bresenham: DDA uses floating point and rounding, Bresenham uses integers only, is faster, and has no accumulated error.

Recap: Bresenham's algorithm steps along the major axis and decides at each step between two candidate pixels using an integer decision parameter. For 0 < m < 1: p0 = 2dy - dx; if p < 0 keep y and add 2dy; otherwise increase y and add 2dy - 2dx. Other slopes use symmetry. It gives the same pixels as careful DDA, with only integer additions. Next we use the same midpoint thinking to draw circles.
key_points: Bresenham (1962) draws lines using only integer additions, subtractions and sign tests.
For 0 < m < 1, x steps by 1 and y either stays or increases by 1.
The decision parameter pk = dx (d1 - d2) compares distances to the two candidate pixels without fractions.
p0 = 2dy - dx; if pk < 0 then p(k+1) = pk + 2dy; else y increases and p(k+1) = pk + 2dy - 2dx.
For (2,3) to (10,8): p values 2, -4, 6, 0, -6, 4, -2, 8 give the same pixels as DDA.
The midpoint view tests which side of the line the midpoint between candidates lies; it leads to the same rules.
Other slopes use symmetry: swap end points, step y by -1, or swap the roles of x and y for |m| > 1.
Compared with DDA it is faster and has no accumulated round-off error.
lessons.tip: Write the three Bresenham rules on a small card: p0 = 2dy - dx, negative adds 2dy, non-negative adds 2dy - 2dx and moves y. Then practise one table a day for a week; it becomes automatic.
lessons.task: Trace Bresenham for the line (0,0) to (8,3) in a table with k, p, and the plotted pixel. Then run DDA on the same line and check that both give the same pixels.

quiz.q: What is the initial decision parameter in Bresenham's algorithm for 0 < m < 1?
quiz.explain: Substituting the start point gives p0 = 2dy - dx.

quiz.q: If pk < 0 for a gentle slope line, what happens next?
options: y stays the same and p increases by 2dy
y increases and p increases by 2dy - 2dx
quiz.explain: A negative p means the lower pixel is closer, so y is unchanged and 2dy is added.

quiz.q: For the line (2,3) to (10,8), what is 2dy - 2dx?
What is the main advantage of Bresenham over DDA?
options: It uses only integer arithmetic and has no accumulated round-off
It works only for vertical lines
quiz.explain: Bresenham avoids floating point and rounding, so it is faster and exact.

quiz.q: How does Bresenham handle a line with slope greater than 1?
options: It swaps the roles of x and y so y becomes the major axis
It draws it as two lines
quiz.explain: For steep lines y steps by 1 every time and x makes the decision.

lessons.title: The Midpoint Circle Algorithm and 8-Way Symmetry
lessons.content:
Think about drawing a round alpona design on the floor for Pohela Boishakh. You tie a string to a nail at the centre, hold chalk at the other end and walk around. The string keeps every chalk point at the same distance from the centre. A computer has no string. It has a grid of square pixels and must decide, for every column, which pixel is closest to that perfect circle. And it must do it fast, because a game may draw hundreds of circles per frame. This lesson shows a beautiful trick: compute only one eighth of the circle with integer additions, and copy it to the other seven eighths for free.

The circle equation: A circle with centre (xc, yc) and radius r is the set of points (x, y) with (x - xc)^2 + (y - yc)^2 = r^2. To keep things simple, we first draw a circle centred at the origin, x^2 + y^2 = r^2, and later shift every pixel by (xc, yc). Shifting is just adding two numbers, so nothing is lost.

Attempt 1, solve for y: From x^2 + y^2 = r^2 we get y = plus or minus the square root of (r^2 - x^2). Step x from -r to r and plot both values. It works but has two problems. Each pixel needs a square root, which is slow. And the spacing is uneven: near the top, where the circle is flat, consecutive pixels touch nicely, but near the left and right sides, where the circle is almost vertical, y changes a lot for each step in x, so the circle shows big gaps.

Attempt 2, use angles: Use x = r cos(theta), y = r sin(theta) and step theta from 0 to 360 degrees. With a small enough step, about 1/r radians, the spacing is even. But each pixel now needs a sine and a cosine, which are even slower than a square root. We want the same quality with only integer additions, just like Bresenham did for lines.

Eight-way symmetry: A circle centred at the origin is symmetric about the x axis, the y axis and the two diagonals y = x and y = -x. So if (x, y) is on the circle, so are (y, x), (-x, y), (-y, x), (x, -y), (y, -x), (-x, -y) and (-y, -x). These eight points come from just one calculation. So we only need to compute one octant, the arc from the top point (0, r) going right until x = y, where the slope of the circle is -1. In that octant, x increases by 1 each step and y either stays or drops by 1, exactly like a gentle-slope line.

The circle function: Define f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - r^2. For any point, f is negative if the point is inside the circle, zero if it is exactly on it, and positive if it is outside. This sign test is the heart of the midpoint method. We do not need to know how far the point is from the circle, only which side it is on.

The midpoint decision: Suppose we have just plotted (xk, yk). The next pixel is either (xk + 1, yk), straight right, or (xk + 1, yk - 1), diagonally down. Look at the midpoint between these two candidates: (xk + 1, yk - 0.5). Compute pk = f(xk + 1, yk - 0.5). If pk < 0, the midpoint is inside the circle, so the true circle passes above the midpoint and the upper pixel yk is closer: keep y. If pk >= 0, the midpoint is on or outside the circle, so the circle passes below it and we choose yk - 1.

The incremental updates: Expanding f at the next midpoint and subtracting gives two simple rules. If pk < 0, then p(k+1) = pk + 2x(k+1) + 1. If pk >= 0, then y decreases and p(k+1) = pk + 2x(k+1) + 1 - 2y(k+1). Here x(k+1) and y(k+1) are the new coordinates. The values 2x and 2y themselves can be updated by adding 2 or subtracting 2 each step, so no multiplication is needed at all.

The starting value: At the start, (x0, y0) = (0, r). The first midpoint is (1, r - 0.5), so p0 = f(1, r - 0.5) = 1 + (r - 0.5)^2 - r^2 = 5/4 - r. When r is an integer, all later increments are integers, so we can safely round p0 to p0 = 1 - r without changing any decision. This is the version most exams use.

The algorithm in pseudo-code: x = 0; y = r; p = 1 - r; plot8(x, y); while x < y: x = x + 1; if p < 0: p = p + 2*x + 1 else: y = y - 1; p = p + 2*x + 1 - 2*y; plot8(x, y). Here plot8 plots the eight symmetric points, each shifted by the centre (xc, yc).

Worked example, r = 10: p0 = 1 - 10 = -9, start at (0, 10). k = 0: p = -9 < 0, so plot (1, 10); new p = -9 + 2(1) + 1 = -6. k = 1: p = -6 < 0, plot (2, 10); new p = -6 + 5 = -1. k = 2: p = -1 < 0, plot (3, 10); new p = -1 + 7 = 6. k = 3: p = 6 >= 0, so y drops: plot (4, 9); new p = 6 + 2(4) + 1 - 2(9) = -3. k = 4: p = -3 < 0, plot (5, 9); new p = -3 + 11 = 8. k = 5: p = 8 >= 0, plot (6, 8); new p = 8 + 13 - 16 = 5. k = 6: p = 5 >= 0, plot (7, 7); now x = y, so we stop. The first octant pixels are (0,10), (1,10), (2,10), (3,10), (4,9), (5,9), (6,8), (7,7).

Check with the real circle: At x = 4 the true y is the square root of (100 - 16) = 9.17, so 9 is correct. At x = 6, the square root of 64 is exactly 8. At x = 7, the square root of 51 is about 7.14, so 7 is right. The midpoint method picked the nearest pixel every time, using only additions and sign tests.

Using symmetry with a real centre: Suppose the centre is (50, 40) and the octant point is (3, 10). The eight pixels are (53, 50), (60, 43), (47, 50), (40, 43), (53, 30), (60, 37), (47, 30) and (40, 37). In general add xc to every x and yc to every y. One octant of 8 points becomes a full circle of about 56 to 64 pixels, with some duplicates where octants meet, for example at x = y and at the four axis points.

How many steps does an octant take: The octant ends where x = y, which on the true circle is at x = r divided by the square root of 2, about 0.707 r. For r = 10 that is about 7.07, which is why our loop ran 7 steps and stopped at (7,7). For r = 100 it would run about 71 steps, so a full circle of radius 100 costs about 71 loop iterations, each with a couple of additions and one comparison, plus 8 plots per iteration. Compare that with about 628 calls to sine and cosine for the polar method at a step of 1/r. That is the speed-up symmetry and incremental arithmetic buy you.

Keeping 2x and 2y in the table: In exam tables it helps to keep two extra columns, 2x(k+1) and 2y(k+1). After each step, 2x grows by 2. 2y stays the same if p was negative, and shrinks by 2 if p was non-negative. For r = 10 the 2x column reads 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and the 2y column reads 20, 20, 20, 18, 18, 16, 14. Then each new p is just the old p plus 2x plus 1, minus 2y when y moved. This is exactly how the hardware or a tight loop does it, with no multiplication at all.

Why we stop at x = y: In the first octant the circle's slope goes from 0 at the top to -1 at the diagonal. As long as the slope is between 0 and -1, x is the major axis and stepping x by 1 leaves no gaps. Past the diagonal the circle becomes steeper and y would need to be the major axis. But we never go there: symmetry gives us that part for free by swapping x and y.

Circle attributes and filled circles: A thick circle can be drawn as two circles with radii r and r + w and the ring between them filled. A filled disc can be drawn by connecting each symmetric pair with a horizontal span: for each computed (x, y), draw a horizontal line from (xc - x, yc + y) to (xc + x, yc + y), and similarly for the other pairs. This is how simple 2D libraries fill circles quickly.

Real life example 1, a cricket fielding chart: A TV graphic shows the 30-yard circle and the boundary on a stadium map at Mirpur. Both are circles drawn with a known centre and radius in screen pixels. The midpoint algorithm, or a GPU version of the same idea, draws each one, and symmetry means the program really computes only an eighth of each.

Real life example 2, a phone's loading spinner and profile pictures: Apps show round profile photos in Messenger and round progress rings while loading. The round edge of a profile picture is a circle used as a mask, and the progress ring is an arc, a piece of a circle drawn between two angles. Libraries rasterize these edges with incremental circle methods plus antialiasing so the edge looks smooth.

Common mistakes: Using p0 = 5/4 - r and then mixing fractions with integers; for integer r just use 1 - r. Forgetting to update 2x with the new x before adding. Choosing yk - 1 when p is negative; it is the other way round, because negative means the midpoint is inside. Not stopping at x >= y, which duplicates or distorts points. Plotting only four symmetric points instead of eight, which leaves two octants missing.

What exams ask: Derive the midpoint circle decision parameter. State the update rules and the initial value. Trace the algorithm for a given radius, often r = 8 or r = 10, in a table with k, pk, (x, y), 2x and 2y. Explain eight-way symmetry and list the eight points for a given octant point and centre. Compare with the square root and polar methods.

Recap: The midpoint circle algorithm computes one octant from (0, r) until x = y, choosing between (x + 1, y) and (x + 1, y - 1) by the sign of the circle function at the midpoint. p0 = 1 - r; if p < 0 add 2x + 1; otherwise decrease y and add 2x + 1 - 2y. Eight-way symmetry and adding the centre complete the circle. Next lesson we stretch the same idea to ellipses, where symmetry gives only four copies and we need two regions.
key_points: A circle is (x - xc)^2 + (y - yc)^2 = r^2; draw it at the origin and shift every pixel by (xc, yc).
Square root and polar methods are slow, and the square root method leaves gaps near steep parts.
Eight-way symmetry: one computed point (x, y) gives eight points by swapping and negating x and y.
Only the octant from (0, r) to x = y is computed; there x steps by 1 and y stays or drops by 1.
The circle function f = x^2 + y^2 - r^2 is negative inside, zero on, positive outside the circle.
p0 = 1 - r (rounded from 5/4 - r); if p < 0, p += 2x + 1; else y decreases and p += 2x + 1 - 2y.
Filled discs can be drawn by joining symmetric points with horizontal spans.
lessons.tip: When tracing a circle, add one extra column showing the true y = sqrt(r^2 - x^2). It takes seconds on a calculator and instantly confirms each choice.
lessons.task: Trace the midpoint circle algorithm for r = 8 with centre (20, 20). List the first-octant points, then write all eight symmetric pixels for the point where x first equals or passes y.

quiz.q: What is the initial decision parameter of the midpoint circle algorithm for integer r?
quiz.explain: p0 = 5/4 - r, which can be rounded to 1 - r when r is an integer.

quiz.q: If pk < 0, which pixel is chosen next?
quiz.explain: Negative p means the midpoint is inside the circle, so the upper pixel yk is closer.

quiz.q: How many points does one computed point give using circle symmetry?
quiz.explain: A circle at the origin is symmetric about both axes and both diagonals, giving eight points.

quiz.q: For r = 10, which pixel follows (3,10) in the first octant?
quiz.explain: At k = 3, p = 6 >= 0, so y drops: the next pixel is (4,9).

quiz.q: What does f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - r^2 > 0 tell us?
options: The point is on the circle
The point is inside the circle
The point is outside the circle
quiz.explain: A positive circle function means the point is farther than r from the centre.

lessons.title: The Midpoint Ellipse Algorithm: Two Regions, Four Copies
lessons.content:
Look at a round plate of rice from directly above: it is a circle. Now tilt your head and look at the same plate from the side of the table: it becomes an oval, wide but squashed. That oval is an ellipse. Ellipses appear everywhere in graphics: a wheel seen at an angle, a cricket ball's shadow, the orbit of a planet in a school app, an oval button or photo frame. Drawing one is a little harder than drawing a circle, because an ellipse is not equally curved everywhere. In this lesson we extend the midpoint idea from circles to ellipses and work through a full numeric example.

What an ellipse is: An ellipse with centre at the origin and axes along x and y is the set of points satisfying (x / rx)^2 + (y / ry)^2 = 1, where rx is the semi-major or semi-minor radius along x and ry the radius along y. If rx = ry, it is a circle. If rx = 8 and ry = 6, the ellipse is 16 units wide and 12 tall. As with circles, we draw it at the origin and shift each pixel by the centre (xc, yc). Ellipses whose axes are tilted are usually drawn by rotating an axis-aligned ellipse, which we will be able to do after the transformation lessons, so here we stick to axis-aligned ones.

The ellipse function: Multiplying through by rx^2 ry^2 removes the fractions: f(x, y) = ry^2 x^2 + rx^2 y^2 - rx^2 ry^2. Just like the circle function, f is negative inside the ellipse, zero on it and positive outside. The midpoint method again tests the sign of f at the midpoint between two candidate pixels. Everything stays in integers or simple halves.

Only four-way symmetry: A circle is symmetric about both axes and both diagonals, giving 8 copies. An ellipse with different radii is symmetric only about the x axis and the y axis, because swapping x and y would turn a wide ellipse into a tall one. So one computed point (x, y) gives only four points: (x, y), (-x, y), (x, -y) and (-x, -y). We therefore compute a whole quadrant, from the top point (0, ry) down to the right point (rx, 0), and mirror it four ways.

Why two regions: In the first quadrant, starting at the top (0, ry), the ellipse is flat: the slope is close to 0. As we move right, the curve bends down more and more until, at the right end (rx, 0), it is vertical. Somewhere in between the slope passes -1. Before that point x changes faster than y, so x should be the major axis and step by 1. After that point y changes faster, so y should be the major axis and step down by 1. So we split the quadrant into region 1, where we step in x, and region 2, where we step in y.

Finding the boundary: The slope of the ellipse is dy/dx = -(2 ry^2 x) / (2 rx^2 y). The slope equals -1 when 2 ry^2 x = 2 rx^2 y. So we stay in region 1 while 2 ry^2 x < 2 rx^2 y, and switch to region 2 as soon as 2 ry^2 x >= 2 rx^2 y. Nicely, both of these quantities are exactly the increments we keep updating anyway, so the test is free.

Region 1 rules: At (xk, yk), the candidates are (xk + 1, yk) and (xk + 1, yk - 1). The midpoint is (xk + 1, yk - 0.5). The starting decision parameter is p1 = f(1, ry - 0.5) = ry^2 - rx^2 ry + rx^2 / 4. If p1 < 0 the midpoint is inside, keep y, and update p1 = p1 + 2 ry^2 x(k+1) + ry^2. If p1 >= 0 step y down and update p1 = p1 + 2 ry^2 x(k+1) - 2 rx^2 y(k+1) + ry^2. Each step, 2 ry^2 x grows by 2 ry^2, and 2 rx^2 y shrinks by 2 rx^2 whenever y drops.

Region 2 rules: Now y is the major axis. At (xk, yk) the candidates are (xk, yk - 1), straight down, and (xk + 1, yk - 1), diagonally. The midpoint is (xk + 0.5, yk - 1). The starting parameter uses the last point (x0, y0) of region 1: p2 = ry^2 (x0 + 0.5)^2 + rx^2 (y0 - 1)^2 - rx^2 ry^2. If p2 > 0 the midpoint is outside, so the curve passes to the left of it: keep x, and update p2 = p2 - 2 rx^2 y(k+1) + rx^2. If p2 <= 0 step x right too, and update p2 = p2 + 2 ry^2 x(k+1) - 2 rx^2 y(k+1) + rx^2. Continue until y = 0.

Notice the flipped rule: In region 1 a negative parameter means stay on the same row. In region 2 a positive parameter means stay in the same column. In both cases the rule is: if the midpoint is inside, the curve is on the outer side of it, so choose the outer candidate; if outside, choose the inner candidate. Thinking in terms of inside and outside is easier than memorising signs.

The whole algorithm in pseudo-code: x = 0; y = ry; px = 0; py = 2*rx2*y; plot4(x, y); p = ry2 - rx2*ry + rx2/4; while px < py: x = x + 1; px = px + 2*ry2; if p < 0: p = p + ry2 + px else: y = y - 1; py = py - 2*rx2; p = p + ry2 + px - py; plot4(x, y). Then p = ry2*(x + 0.5)^2 + rx2*(y - 1)^2 - rx2*ry2; while y > 0: y = y - 1; py = py - 2*rx2; if p > 0: p = p + rx2 - py else: x = x + 1; px = px + 2*ry2; p = p + rx2 - py + px; plot4(x, y). Here rx2 and ry2 are rx^2 and ry^2 computed once, px and py hold 2 ry^2 x and 2 rx^2 y, and plot4 draws the four mirrored pixels shifted by the centre.

Worked example, rx = 8, ry = 6: Here rx^2 = 64, ry^2 = 36, so 2 rx^2 = 128 and 2 ry^2 = 72. Start at (0, 6). The initial region 1 parameter is p1 = 36 - 64 x 6 + 64/4 = 36 - 384 + 16 = -332. Initially 2 ry^2 x = 0 and 2 rx^2 y = 128 x 6 = 768.

Region 1 trace: k = 0: p = -332 < 0, plot (1, 6); now 2 ry^2 x = 72, 2 rx^2 y = 768; new p = -332 + 72 + 36 = -224. k = 1: p = -224, plot (2, 6); 144, 768; new p = -224 + 144 + 36 = -44. k = 2: p = -44, plot (3, 6); 216, 768; new p = -44 + 216 + 36 = 208. k = 3: p = 208 >= 0, plot (4, 5); 288, 640; new p = 208 + 288 - 640 + 36 = -108. k = 4: p = -108, plot (5, 5); 360, 640; new p = -108 + 360 + 36 = 288. k = 5: p = 288, plot (6, 4); 432, 512; new p = 288 + 432 - 512 + 36 = 244. k = 6: p = 244, plot (7, 3); 504, 384. Now 504 >= 384, so region 1 ends at (7, 3).

Region 2 trace: The starting parameter is p2 = 36 x (7.5)^2 + 64 x (3 - 1)^2 - 64 x 36 = 2025 + 256 - 2304 = -23. k = 0: p = -23 <= 0, so x also steps: plot (8, 2); now 2 ry^2 x = 576 and 2 rx^2 y = 256; new p = -23 + 576 - 256 + 64 = 361. k = 1: p = 361 > 0, keep x: plot (8, 1); 2 rx^2 y = 128; new p = 361 - 128 + 64 = 297. k = 2: p = 297 > 0, plot (8, 0). y has reached 0, so we stop.

The full quadrant: (0,6), (1,6), (2,6), (3,6), (4,5), (5,5), (6,4), (7,3), (8,2), (8,1), (8,0). Check a few with the real ellipse y = 6 times the square root of (1 - x^2/64): at x = 4, y is about 5.20, so 5 is right; at x = 6, y is about 3.97, so 4 is right; at x = 7, y is about 2.90, so 3 is right. Mirroring gives the other three quadrants; with centre (xc, yc), add it to each.

Cost and precision: Just like the circle, every step is a few additions and a sign test. The only non-integer value is rx^2 / 4 in p1 and the 0.5 in p2. Many implementations multiply all parameters by 4 to keep everything integer, or simply round p1, which rarely changes a decision. For exams, use the formulas as given and keep the fraction where it appears; in our example rx^2 / 4 = 16 was already an integer.

Circle versus ellipse side by side: Both start at the top of the curve and use a midpoint sign test with integer increments. The circle computes one octant and copies it 8 ways, stopping at x = y. The ellipse computes a full quadrant and copies it 4 ways, and because it has no diagonal symmetry it must handle the steep part itself with region 2. Set rx = ry = r in the ellipse formulas and divide by r^2, and you get back the circle rules, so the circle is really a special case. The ellipse also needs larger numbers, because rx^2 ry^2 grows fast, which matters on hardware with small integer registers.

Real life example 1, a stadium on a sports app: Sports apps show cricket grounds as ovals because most real grounds, including many in Bangladesh, are not perfect circles. The boundary rope is drawn as an ellipse with a horizontal radius larger than the vertical one. The app supplies the centre and two radii, and a midpoint ellipse routine or a GPU path renderer produces the pixels.

Real life example 2, a 3D wheel on screen: A rickshaw wheel seen from the front is a thin line, from the side a circle, and from an angle an ellipse. When a game shows a wheel turned slightly toward the camera, its rim projects onto the screen as an ellipse. In 3D engines the triangles of the wheel are projected rather than calling an ellipse routine, but 2D drawing tools, charts and UI libraries still draw ellipses directly with incremental methods like this one.

Common mistakes: Using 8-way symmetry for an ellipse; that works only for circles. Forgetting to switch regions, which makes the curve gappy near the sides. Using the region 1 starting value in region 2 instead of recomputing p2 from the last point. Mixing up which radius goes with x: f has ry^2 multiplying x^2, not rx^2. And swapping the meaning of the sign in region 2.

What exams ask: Derive the decision parameters for both regions. State the condition for changing regions. Trace the algorithm for given rx and ry, very often rx = 8 and ry = 6, in two tables. Explain why only four-way symmetry applies. Compare the midpoint circle and ellipse algorithms.

Recap: An axis-aligned ellipse is drawn one quadrant at a time and mirrored four ways. Region 1 steps x while 2 ry^2 x < 2 rx^2 y, with p1 = ry^2 - rx^2 ry + rx^2/4. Region 2 steps y down to 0, with p2 computed from the last region 1 point. Each choice tests whether the midpoint is inside or outside. With these three raster algorithms done, next we fill whole areas: polygons by scan lines.
key_points: An axis-aligned ellipse is (x/rx)^2 + (y/ry)^2 = 1; the ellipse function f = ry^2 x^2 + rx^2 y^2 - rx^2 ry^2 is negative inside.
Ellipses have only four-way symmetry, so a whole quadrant is computed and mirrored.
Region 1 (slope magnitude below 1) steps x; region 2 steps y; switch when 2 ry^2 x >= 2 rx^2 y.
Region 1 starts with p1 = ry^2 - rx^2 ry + rx^2/4 at (0, ry).
Region 2 starts with p2 = ry^2 (x0 + 0.5)^2 + rx^2 (y0 - 1)^2 - rx^2 ry^2 from the last region 1 point.
If the midpoint is inside choose the outer candidate; if outside choose the inner one.
All steps use additions and sign tests; 2 ry^2 x and 2 rx^2 y are updated incrementally.
lessons.tip: Remember the region rule by picture, not by formula: at the top the ellipse is flat (walk sideways), at the side it is steep (walk downwards). The switch happens where the curve is at 45 degrees.
lessons.task: Trace the midpoint ellipse algorithm for rx = 6, ry = 4. Find where region 1 ends, compute p2, and list the whole first quadrant. Then plot all four quadrants on graph paper with centre (10, 10).

quiz.q: How many symmetric points does one computed point give for an ellipse with rx != ry?
quiz.explain: An ellipse is symmetric only about the two axes, so (x,y), (-x,y), (x,-y), (-x,-y).

quiz.q: When does the algorithm switch from region 1 to region 2?
quiz.explain: The slope magnitude reaches 1 when 2 ry^2 x = 2 rx^2 y.

quiz.q: For rx = 8, ry = 6, what is the initial region 1 decision parameter?
In region 2, if p2 > 0, what is the next pixel?
quiz.explain: A positive p2 means the midpoint is outside, so x stays and y steps down.

quiz.q: In the rx = 8, ry = 6 example, at which point does region 1 end?
quiz.explain: At (7,3), 2 ry^2 x = 504 >= 2 rx^2 y = 384, so region 2 begins.

lessons.title: Scan-Line Polygon Fill: Inside Tests, Edge Tables and Active Edges
lessons.content:
Imagine painting the walls of a room with a roller. You do not dab paint pixel by pixel; you roll a long horizontal stroke from one edge of the wall to the other, move a little lower, and roll again. Where there is a window in the middle of the wall, each stroke stops at the window frame and starts again after it. That is exactly how the scan-line fill algorithm colours a polygon: one horizontal row at a time, finding where the row enters and leaves the shape, and filling between those points.

Why filling matters: Lines and circles give outlines, but most of what we see on screens is filled area: the coloured map of Bangladesh's divisions in a textbook app, bars in a chart, buttons, and above all the triangles that make every 3D model. A modern GPU fills billions of triangle pixels per second. Filling is therefore one of the most important raster operations, and the scan-line method is its classic form.

Polygons: A polygon is a closed shape made of straight edges joining a list of vertices, for example A(1,1), B(9,1), C(9,7), D(5,3), E(1,7), with the last vertex joined back to the first. A polygon is convex if every interior angle is less than 180 degrees; equivalently, the line segment between any two inside points stays inside. Triangles, rectangles and regular hexagons are convex. A polygon is concave if it has a dent, like our example, where vertex D pokes inward. Concave polygons are harder because one horizontal row can enter and leave the shape more than once.

The inside question: Before filling, we need a rule for whether a point is inside. For simple polygons this is obvious, but for polygons whose edges cross themselves, like a five-pointed star drawn in one stroke, there are two standard rules. Graphics libraries let you choose between them, so you must know both.

The even-odd rule: From the point, draw a ray in any direction that does not pass through a vertex, and count how many polygon edges it crosses. If the count is odd, the point is inside; if even, outside. For a point in the middle of a square, a ray to the right crosses one edge: odd, inside. For a point to the left of the square, the ray crosses two edges: even, outside. For a one-stroke star, the central pentagon is crossed twice by a ray, so it counts as outside and appears as a hole.

The nonzero winding rule: Give each edge a direction, following the order of vertices. Draw the ray again, and add +1 when an edge crosses it going one way (say upward) and -1 when an edge crosses it going the other way. If the total, called the winding number, is not zero, the point is inside. For the one-stroke star, the central pentagon has winding number 2, so it is inside and the whole star is filled. For simple polygons, both rules agree; they differ only for self-intersecting shapes.

The scan-line idea: Take the polygon and sweep a horizontal line, a scan line, from the lowest y to the highest y. For each scan line: find all points where it crosses polygon edges; sort those x values from left to right; then fill pixels between the first and second intersection, between the third and fourth, and so on. Pairing works because a horizontal line enters and leaves the shape alternately, which is the even-odd rule applied along the row.

Computing intersections: An edge from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2) crosses the scan line y at x = x1 + (y - y1)(x2 - x1)/(y2 - y1). For edge D(5,3) to E(1,7) and scan line y = 5: x = 5 + (5 - 3)(1 - 5)/(7 - 3) = 5 + 2 x (-1) = 3. For edge C(9,7) to D(5,3): x = 9 + (5 - 7)(5 - 9)/(3 - 7) = 9 + (-2)(-4)/(-4) = 7. Edges E to A and B to C are vertical at x = 1 and x = 9. Edge A to B is horizontal and ignored, because a horizontal edge never crosses a scan line at a single point.

Worked scan line y = 5: The intersections are 1, 3, 7 and 9. Sorted, they pair up as (1, 3) and (7, 9). So on row 5 we fill x = 1 to 3 and x = 7 to 9, and leave the dent between 4 and 6 empty. That is the window in our wall-painting story. On row 2, below the dent, only the two vertical edges are crossed, giving one span from 1 to 9.

The vertex problem: What if the scan line passes exactly through a vertex? At y = 3 the scan line hits vertex D, which belongs to two edges, CD and DE. If we count D once, we get the list 1, 5, 9, an odd count, and pairing breaks. The rule is: if the two edges meeting at the vertex go to opposite sides of the scan line (one up, one down), count the vertex once; if they both go up or both go down (a local minimum or maximum), count it twice. At D both edges go up, so D counts twice: 1, 5, 5, 9, giving spans (1, 5) and (5, 9), the full row, which is correct because the dent's tip is just a point.

The neat practical trick: Implementations handle all vertex cases automatically by treating each edge's y range as half-open: an edge covers ymin up to but not including ymax. At a local minimum both edges start there, so the vertex is counted twice. At a local maximum both edges end there, so it is counted zero times, still even. At a monotone vertex, one edge ends and the other starts, so it is counted exactly once. One rule, no special cases. The side effect is that the topmost row of a polygon is not filled, which is actually desirable: two polygons sharing an edge will not both paint the shared row.

Using coherence: Recomputing every edge's intersection with the formula on every row is wasteful. Notice that if an edge crosses row y at x, it crosses row y + 1 at x + 1/m, where 1/m = (x2 - x1)/(y2 - y1) is the change in x per row. This is edge coherence, the same incremental trick as DDA. Also, the set of edges crossed changes only at vertex rows. This is scan-line coherence.

The edge table: Before scanning, build an edge table (ET): one bucket for each scan line, holding the edges whose lower end (ymin) is on that row. For each edge store three numbers: ymax, the x at ymin, and 1/m. Horizontal edges are left out. For our polygon: bucket y = 1 holds E-A (ymax 7, x 1, 1/m 0) and B-C (ymax 7, x 9, 1/m 0); bucket y = 3 holds D-E (ymax 7, x 5, 1/m -1) and C-D (ymax 7, x 5, 1/m +1).

The active edge list: While scanning we keep an active edge list (AEL) of edges that cross the current row, sorted by x. For each row y: move the edges from bucket y of the ET into the AEL; remove edges whose ymax equals y; sort by x; fill between pairs; then add 1/m to each edge's x for the next row. Trace: y = 1 and 2: AEL x = 1, 9, fill 1 to 9. y = 3: D-E and C-D join at x = 5, AEL 1, 5, 5, 9. y = 4: x values 1, 4, 6, 9, spans 1 to 4 and 6 to 9. y = 5: 1, 3, 7, 9. y = 6: 1, 2, 8, 9. y = 7: all edges reach ymax and leave. The dent shows up as a gap that narrows to a point at D.

The algorithm in pseudo-code: build ET; AEL = empty; for y = ymin_of_polygon to ymax_of_polygon: append ET[y] to AEL; remove from AEL every edge with ymax == y; sort AEL by x; for each pair (e1, e2) in AEL: fill pixels from ceil(e1.x) to floor(e2.x) on row y; for each edge e in AEL: e.x = e.x + e.invSlope. The rounding at span ends, ceil on the left and floor on the right, keeps the fill inside the true edges. Because the AEL changes only a little from one row to the next, a simple insertion sort keeps it ordered very cheaply.

Another way, testing pixels with edge functions: For a triangle, a GPU can also test each pixel in the bounding box directly. For an edge from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2), the edge function E(x, y) = (x - x1)(y2 - y1) - (y - y1)(x2 - x1) is positive on one side of the edge and negative on the other. A pixel is inside the triangle if all three edge functions have the same sign. These functions also change by constant amounts from pixel to pixel, so they are incremental too, and they are easy to compute in parallel for many pixels at once, which suits GPU hardware.

Pixel ownership: Real rasterizers decide carefully which pixels to fill at the span ends, for example filling a pixel only if its centre is inside, and using a top-left rule for pixels exactly on an edge, so that two triangles sharing an edge never paint the same pixel twice and never leave a crack. This is why GPU-rendered meshes have no gaps or double-blended seams.

Real life example 1, a district map in an education app: A map of Bangladesh's 64 districts stores each district as a polygon of hundreds of vertices, many concave, like the coastline districts. When you tap Khulna to highlight it, the app fills that polygon with a colour using a scan-line or similar polygon filler. The even-odd or nonzero rule also handles islands and holes, such as a lake inside a region.

Real life example 2, 3D games: Every frame of a mobile game is mostly filled triangles. Triangles are convex, so each row has exactly one span, which makes GPU filling simple and fast. Complex polygons are first split into triangles, called triangulation, and then filled. So the scan-line ideas, edges, increments and spans, live inside every GPU.

Common mistakes: Not sorting intersections before pairing. Counting a local minimum vertex once and getting an odd list. Including horizontal edges in the edge table, which divides by zero when computing 1/m. Forgetting to update x by 1/m for each row. Mixing up the even-odd and nonzero winding rules for self-intersecting shapes.

What exams ask: Explain the scan-line polygon fill algorithm with edge table and active edge list. Show the intersections for a given scan line and the spans filled. Explain how vertices are handled. Distinguish even-odd and nonzero winding rules with a star example. Define convex and concave polygons. Explain edge and scan-line coherence.

Recap: A polygon is filled row by row: find edge intersections, sort, pair, and fill spans. The even-odd and nonzero winding rules define inside for tricky shapes. Vertices are counted once or twice depending on the edge directions, which the half-open rule handles automatically. The edge table and active edge list use coherence to update intersections by adding 1/m per row. Next lesson covers the other family of fill methods, seed fills like flood fill and boundary fill, plus how to smooth jagged edges.
key_points: A polygon is convex if every interior angle is under 180 degrees; concave polygons have dents and can give several spans per row.
Even-odd rule: a ray crossing an odd number of edges means inside.
Nonzero winding rule: sum +1 and -1 for directed edge crossings; nonzero means inside; it differs from even-odd only for self-intersecting shapes.
