Scan-line fill: for each row find intersections, sort them, pair them and fill the spans between pairs.
A vertex is counted twice at a local minimum or maximum and once when its edges go to opposite sides; half-open edge ranges handle this automatically.
Edge coherence: x for the next row is x + 1/m.
The edge table buckets edges by ymin with (ymax, x, 1/m); the active edge list holds edges crossing the current row.
GPUs fill triangles, which are convex and give one span per row; complex polygons are triangulated first.
lessons.tip: When you trace a scan-line fill, draw the polygon on graph paper and literally draw each scan line with a ruler. Write the sorted intersection list beside each line before colouring spans.
lessons.task: On graph paper draw the L-shaped polygon (2,1), (10,1), (10,4), (5,4), (5,8), (2,8). Build its edge table (leave out horizontal edges), then trace the active edge list row by row from y = 1 to y = 7 and colour the spans.

quiz.q: Using the even-odd rule, a ray from a point crosses 3 edges. The point is:
quiz.explain: An odd number of crossings means the point is inside.

quiz.q: For the scan line y = 5 in the lesson's polygon, which spans are filled?
quiz.explain: Sorted intersections 1, 3, 7, 9 pair as (1,3) and (7,9).

quiz.q: What does each edge table entry typically store?
quiz.explain: These three values let the active edge list update x incrementally.

quiz.q: How should a vertex that is a local minimum be counted?
quiz.explain: Both edges go up from it, so it is counted twice to keep the intersection count even.

quiz.q: Why are horizontal edges left out of the edge table?
options: They do not cross a scan line at a single point and 1/m would divide by zero
They are drawn in a different colour
They only appear in convex polygons
quiz.explain: A horizontal edge lies along a scan line; its span is covered by the neighbouring edges.

lessons.title: Flood Fill, Boundary Fill and Antialiasing
lessons.content:
Pour a glass of water onto the middle of a tiled floor surrounded by a small border of bricks. The water spreads from tile to neighbouring tile until it reaches the bricks, then stops. It does not need to know the shape of the border in advance; it just keeps spreading while it can. The paint bucket tool in MS Paint or any phone drawing app works exactly like this. You tap one point, called the seed, and the colour spreads to connected neighbours. This lesson covers these seed fill methods, and then a second problem every raster picture has: jagged edges, and how antialiasing smooths them.

Two families of fill: In the last lesson the scan-line algorithm filled a polygon from its edge list: it knew the geometry. Seed fills are different. They work directly on pixels in the frame buffer, starting from one point known to be inside, and they need no list of edges. That makes them ideal for interactive painting programs, where the region might be any hand-drawn shape, and for filling areas in images rather than in geometric descriptions.

Boundary fill: In boundary fill, the region is defined by a boundary colour. Starting from the seed, we colour the pixel and spread to neighbours, stopping at pixels that already have the boundary colour or the fill colour. In pseudo-code: boundaryFill4(x, y, fill, boundary): c = getPixel(x, y); if c != boundary and c != fill: setPixel(x, y, fill); boundaryFill4(x + 1, y, fill, boundary); boundaryFill4(x - 1, y, fill, boundary); boundaryFill4(x, y + 1, fill, boundary); boundaryFill4(x, y - 1, fill, boundary). The check against the fill colour is essential; without it the algorithm would revisit already coloured pixels forever.

Flood fill: In flood fill, the region is defined by its current interior colour, not by a boundary. Starting from the seed with old colour, we recolour every connected pixel that has exactly that old colour. In pseudo-code: floodFill4(x, y, fill, old): if getPixel(x, y) == old: setPixel(x, y, fill); then the same four recursive calls. Use flood fill when the area has one uniform colour but its border is made of several different colours, for example recolouring a white sky surrounded by green trees, brown hills and a blue river. Boundary fill would need a single boundary colour, which this picture does not have.

A small trace: Suppose a boundary encloses a 3 x 3 block of 9 white pixels and we call boundaryFill4 on the centre. The centre is coloured and calls its four neighbours; each edge-middle pixel is coloured and calls its neighbours, which reach the corners; and so on. In total 9 pixels are coloured. Counting calls, the first call plus 4 calls from each of the 9 coloured pixels makes 1 + 36 = 37 calls, and 28 of them return immediately because they hit the boundary or an already filled pixel. Seed fills do a lot of checking, which is their main cost.

Four-connected and eight-connected: There are two ways to define neighbours. In a 4-connected fill, a pixel's neighbours are left, right, up and down. In an 8-connected fill, the four diagonal pixels are neighbours too. The difference matters at thin diagonal boundaries. Imagine a boundary drawn as a diagonal staircase of pixels, touching only at corners. A 4-connected fill cannot step diagonally, so it stays inside. An 8-connected fill can slip between two corner-touching boundary pixels and leak to the outside, flooding the whole screen. Rule to remember: a 4-connected fill needs a boundary that is at least 8-connected; an 8-connected fill needs a boundary that is 4-connected. On the other hand, an 8-connected fill can reach into narrow diagonal corridors that a 4-connected fill would miss.

The recursion problem: The recursive versions are short and easy to understand, but each call uses stack memory. Filling a 1000 x 1000 region could create a chain of recursive calls hundreds of thousands deep, and most programs would crash with a stack overflow long before that. Real implementations therefore use an explicit stack or queue: push the seed; while the stack is not empty, pop a pixel, and if it should be filled, colour it and push its neighbours. This is just depth-first or breadth-first search on the grid graph, which you met in Data Structures.

Scan-line seed fill: A smarter approach fills whole horizontal spans instead of single pixels. From the seed, move left and right until the boundary to find the full span on that row, and fill it in one go. Then look at the row above and the row below across that span; for each separate run of fillable pixels there, push one new seed. Repeat. This pushes far fewer pixels onto the stack, works row by row like the frame buffer itself, and is the kind of method used in practical paint bucket tools.

Stack or queue, does it matter: With an explicit stack (last in, first out) the fill races deep in one direction before coming back, like a person exploring one corridor to its end. With a queue (first in, first out) it spreads in rings around the seed, like ripples in a pond after you drop a stone. Both colour exactly the same pixels in the end. The difference is the order, which you can see in slow animated demos, and the peak memory: the queue holds the current ring of frontier pixels, while the stack can hold a long trail. Many paint programs also mark visited pixels in a separate bit array so a pixel is never pushed twice.

Seed fill versus scan-line polygon fill: Scan-line fill needs the polygon's vertex list and works even before anything is drawn, so it is the choice for geometric rendering, CAD and GPUs. Seed fill needs only the picture and one interior point, so it is the choice for paint programs and image editing. Scan-line fill visits each interior pixel once and in order, which is fast and memory friendly. Seed fill checks each pixel several times and needs a stack, but it handles any shape the user can draw, including shapes with curved or hand-drawn borders that have no vertex list at all.

Pattern fill: Instead of a single colour, an area can be filled with a pattern, like the checks of a lungi or bricks on a wall. A small pattern array of size w x h is tiled across the plane: the colour for pixel (x, y) is pattern[x mod w][y mod h]. Because it uses the absolute pixel position, neighbouring shapes filled with the same pattern line up perfectly, like tiles on a floor.

Aliasing, the jaggies: Every raster algorithm we have studied decides, for each pixel, fully on or fully off. A smooth diagonal edge then appears as a staircase, the effect called the jaggies. More generally, aliasing is what happens when a continuous signal is sampled too coarsely: fine detail turns into false patterns. On screens you see it as stair-stepped edges, as small objects flickering in and out as they move, and as shimmering moire patterns on fine stripes like a striped shirt on TV. In animation, a turning wheel can appear to spin backwards, a temporal form of aliasing.

Why it happens: A pixel is a sample of the picture at one point. An edge that passes through the middle of a pixel can only be represented as on or off, so information about where exactly the edge lies is lost. The fix is not to make pixels smaller forever, which costs memory and bandwidth, but to let a pixel's colour reflect how much of it is covered. This is antialiasing.

Supersampling: The simplest antialiasing method computes the image at a higher resolution and averages down. For example, divide each pixel into a 3 x 3 grid of 9 subpixels, decide for each subpixel whether it is inside the shape, and set the pixel's intensity to the fraction covered. If 4 of 9 subsamples are inside a black line on a white background, the pixel becomes 4/9 black: its grey value is 255 x (1 - 4/9), about 142. Edge pixels become shades of grey, and the eye sees a smooth line. The cost is 9 times the sampling work for 3 x 3, or 4 times for 2 x 2.

Area sampling: Instead of counting subsamples, area sampling treats the line or edge as a shape with real width and computes the exact area of each pixel square it covers. If a one-pixel-wide line covers 30 percent of a pixel, that pixel gets 30 percent intensity. Weighted area sampling goes further and lets coverage near the pixel centre count more than coverage near its corners, using a filter shaped like a small cone or bell. This gives the smoothest results but costs the most computation.

Antialiasing in practice: Xiaolin Wu's line algorithm (1991) draws antialiased lines quickly by plotting two pixels per column with intensities split according to the distance from the true line. GPUs offer multisample antialiasing (MSAA), which tests coverage at several sample points per pixel but runs the expensive colour calculation only once per pixel. Fonts on your phone are rendered with antialiasing, which is why letters look smooth even on modest screens. The trade-off is always quality against speed and a slight softening of the image.

Real life example 1, recolouring a map in a school project: A student in Rajshahi scans a black-and-white outline map of Bangladesh and uses the paint bucket to colour each division. Clicking inside Rajshahi division with a 4-connected flood fill colours it neatly. If the scanned border has a tiny one-pixel gap, the colour leaks into the neighbouring division, a perfect demonstration of why fills need closed boundaries.

Real life example 2, cricket score graphics on TV: The thin diagonal stripes and slanted text of a score banner would look jagged and shimmer on a big LED wall at the stadium without antialiasing. Broadcast graphics systems render with supersampling or similar methods so that edges look clean even when the banner slides across the screen.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the not-already-filled check in boundary fill, causing infinite recursion. Using boundary fill when the border has many colours. Using an 8-connected fill with a boundary that is only 8-connected, so it leaks. Writing deep recursion for large regions. Thinking antialiasing increases resolution; it only changes intensities of edge pixels.

What exams ask: Write boundary fill and flood fill algorithms and explain the difference. Explain 4-connected versus 8-connected fills with a diagram, including the leak problem. Explain why recursive fills can overflow the stack. Define aliasing and list its effects. Explain supersampling and area sampling with a small numeric example.

Recap: Seed fills start from an interior point and spread through neighbours: boundary fill stops at a boundary colour, flood fill replaces one interior colour. 4-connected and 8-connected neighbourhoods behave differently at diagonal boundaries. Practical fills use explicit stacks and spans. Aliasing creates jaggies and moire because pixels are samples; antialiasing sets edge intensities by coverage using supersampling or area sampling. Next we move from drawing to moving: 2D transformations.
key_points: Seed fills start from one interior point and spread through neighbouring pixels.
Boundary fill stops at a given boundary colour; flood fill recolours all connected pixels of one old interior colour.
4-connected uses left, right, up, down; 8-connected adds diagonals and can leak through diagonal-only boundaries.
Recursive fills can overflow the stack; real code uses an explicit stack or queue, often filling whole spans.
Pattern fill uses pattern[x mod w][y mod h] so tiled patterns line up.
Aliasing (jaggies, moire, flicker, backward wheels) comes from sampling a continuous picture at discrete pixels.
Supersampling averages several subsamples per pixel; 4 of 9 covered gives about 44 percent intensity.
Area sampling sets intensity by the area of the pixel covered; weighted area sampling favours the centre.
lessons.tip: Draw a staircase boundary on graph paper and try both 4-connected and 8-connected fills from a seed inside. Seeing the 8-connected fill escape through the corners will fix the rule in your memory.
lessons.task: Open any paint app on your phone or computer, draw a closed shape with a tiny gap and use the bucket tool inside it. Then close the gap and fill again. Finally zoom into a diagonal line drawn with smoothing on and off and note the grey edge pixels.

quiz.q: Which fill should you use to recolour a white area whose border has several different colours?
quiz.explain: Flood fill replaces one interior colour and does not need a single boundary colour.

quiz.q: Why can an 8-connected fill leak through a diagonal staircase boundary?
options: It moves diagonally between corner-touching boundary pixels
quiz.explain: Diagonal neighbours let the fill slip between pixels that touch only at corners.

quiz.q: With 3 x 3 supersampling, 4 subsamples of a pixel are inside a black line on white. What fraction of black is the pixel?
quiz.explain: Coverage is 4 of 9 subsamples, so the pixel is 4/9 black.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of a deeply recursive flood fill on a large region?
quiz.explain: Each recursive call uses stack memory; large regions can exceed the stack.

quiz.q: What is aliasing in raster graphics?
options: Giving two names to a variable
Errors from sampling a continuous image too coarsely, such as jaggies
quiz.explain: Undersampling turns smooth edges and fine detail into stair steps and false patterns.

lessons.title: 2D Transformations and Homogeneous Matrices
lessons.content:
Open the Ludo app on your phone. Your token jumps forward six squares: it moved. Pinch the board and it gets bigger: it scaled. Turn your phone sideways and the whole picture swings round: it rotated. Look at a reflection of the board in a mirror: it flipped. These four everyday actions are the basic geometric transformations of computer graphics. Every game, map and drawing app uses them thousands of times per second. In this lesson we write each one as a small formula, then pack them all into one uniform tool: a 3 x 3 matrix using homogeneous coordinates.

What a transformation is: A geometric transformation is a rule that takes every point (x, y) of an object and gives a new point (x', y'). We never transform pixels one by one for geometric objects; we transform the defining points, the vertices, and then redraw the shape. A triangle has 3 vertices, so moving a triangle means transforming just 3 points. A 3D character with 50,000 vertices is transformed the same way, just with more points.

Translation: Translation moves every point by the same amount: x' = x + tx, y' = y + ty. The pair (tx, ty) is the translation vector. Example: move the point (3, 4) by (5, -2): x' = 3 + 5 = 8, y' = 4 - 2 = 2, so the new point is (8, 2). Translation keeps size, shape and orientation; it only changes position. It is a rigid-body motion.

Scaling: Scaling about the origin multiplies coordinates: x' = sx x, y' = sy y. If sx = sy, it is uniform scaling and the shape keeps its proportions. If they differ, it is differential scaling and the shape stretches. Example: scale (4, 6) by sx = 2, sy = 0.5: x' = 8, y' = 3. A scale factor above 1 enlarges, between 0 and 1 shrinks. One surprise: scaling about the origin also moves the object. A square from (2, 2) to (4, 4), scaled by 2, becomes a square from (4, 4) to (8, 8): bigger, but also further away. To scale an object in place, we will need a composite transform in the next lesson.

Rotation: Rotation about the origin by angle theta, counterclockwise for positive theta, is x' = x cos(theta) - y sin(theta), y' = x sin(theta) + y cos(theta). Where does this come from? Write the point in polar form, x = r cos(phi), y = r sin(phi). Rotating adds theta to the angle: x' = r cos(phi + theta), y' = r sin(phi + theta). Expanding with the angle sum formulas gives exactly the equations above. Example: rotate (3, 4) by 90 degrees. cos 90 = 0, sin 90 = 1, so x' = 0 - 4 = -4 and y' = 3 + 0 = 3: the point (-4, 3). Its distance from the origin is still 5, as it should be.

A rotation with a less friendly angle: Rotate (2, 1) by 30 degrees. cos 30 is about 0.866 and sin 30 = 0.5. x' = 2(0.866) - 1(0.5) = 1.232, y' = 2(0.5) + 1(0.866) = 1.866. Check: the original length is the square root of 5, about 2.236, and the new length is the square root of (1.232^2 + 1.866^2) = the square root of 5.0. Rotation preserves lengths and angles; it is also rigid.

Reflection: Reflection flips an object over a mirror line. About the x axis: (x, y) becomes (x, -y). About the y axis: (-x, y). About the origin: (-x, -y), which is the same as a 180 degree rotation. About the line y = x: (y, x), the coordinates swap. Example: reflect (5, 2) about y = x to get (2, 5). Reflections keep shape and size but reverse orientation: a clockwise list of vertices becomes counterclockwise, which matters later for back-face culling.

Shear: Shear slants an object, like pushing the top of a stack of exercise books sideways. An x-direction shear is x' = x + shx y, y' = y. Points higher up move further sideways. Example: the unit square's top-right corner (1, 1) with shx = 2 goes to (3, 1), while the bottom corners stay put; the square becomes a parallelogram. A y-direction shear is x' = x, y' = y + shy x. Italic text is roughly a small x shear of upright letters.

Why matrices: Scaling, rotation, reflection and shear are all linear: each can be written as a 2 x 2 matrix times the column vector (x, y). For example rotation is the matrix with rows (cos, -sin) and (sin, cos). Linear Algebra showed you that applying one matrix and then another is the same as applying their product. That is a huge saving: a long chain of transforms can be multiplied once into a single matrix, then applied to thousands of vertices. But translation spoils the party: x + tx is not a 2 x 2 matrix times (x, y), because a linear map always sends the origin to itself, while translation moves it.

Homogeneous coordinates: The fix is to add a third coordinate. Represent the point (x, y) as the column (x, y, 1). In general (x, y, h) with h not zero represents the point (x/h, y/h), so (2, 3, 1) and (4, 6, 2) are the same point; for now we always use h = 1. With this extra 1, translation becomes a matrix product: the 3 x 3 matrix with rows (1, 0, tx), (0, 1, ty), (0, 0, 1) times (x, y, 1) gives (x + tx, y + ty, 1). The tx and ty sit in the last column and are multiplied by the 1.

The five matrices in homogeneous form: Translation T(tx, ty): rows (1, 0, tx), (0, 1, ty), (0, 0, 1). Scaling S(sx, sy): rows (sx, 0, 0), (0, sy, 0), (0, 0, 1). Rotation R(theta): rows (cos, -sin, 0), (sin, cos, 0), (0, 0, 1). Reflection about the x axis: rows (1, 0, 0), (0, -1, 0), (0, 0, 1). X shear: rows (1, shx, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1). Every 2D transform we need is now a 3 x 3 matrix, and every combination is a matrix product.

A matrix worked example: Rotate (3, 4) by 90 degrees using the homogeneous matrix. R(90) has rows (0, -1, 0), (1, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1). Multiply row by column: first row gives 0 x 3 + (-1) x 4 + 0 x 1 = -4; second row gives 1 x 3 + 0 x 4 + 0 = 3; third row gives 1. Result (-4, 3, 1), the point (-4, 3), matching our earlier answer. Now translate (3, 4) by (5, -2): rows (1, 0, 5), (0, 1, -2), (0, 0, 1) times (3, 4, 1) gives (8, 2, 1).

Transforming a whole shape: Take the triangle A(0, 0), B(4, 0), C(0, 3). Rotate it by 90 degrees: A stays (0, 0), B(4, 0) goes to (0, 4), C(0, 3) goes to (-3, 0). Put the three points as columns of a 3 x 3 matrix, with a row of ones at the bottom, and a single matrix multiplication transforms all of them at once. This is how graphics hardware thinks: one matrix, many vertices.

Inverse transforms: Every basic transform can be undone. The inverse of T(tx, ty) is T(-tx, -ty). The inverse of S(sx, sy) is S(1/sx, 1/sy), as long as neither is zero. The inverse of R(theta) is R(-theta), and because rotation matrices are orthogonal, the inverse is also simply the transpose. Inverses are used to move a camera, to undo edits, and to map a mouse click on screen back to a point on the object.

Families of transforms: Translations, rotations and reflections are rigid-body transforms: they preserve all lengths and angles. Adding uniform scaling gives similarity transforms, which preserve shape and angles but not size, like a photo enlarged without stretching. Allowing differential scaling and shear gives affine transforms, which keep straight lines straight and parallel lines parallel, but can change angles and lengths: a square can become a parallelogram, never a trapezium. Every 3 x 3 homogeneous matrix whose bottom row is (0, 0, 1) is affine. Because affine transforms keep lines straight, transforming just the end points of a line and then drawing between them gives the correct result, which is exactly why we transform vertices rather than pixels.

What the determinant tells you: The determinant of the upper-left 2 x 2 part says how area changes. For S(2, 0.5) it is 2 x 0.5 = 1, so area stays the same even though the shape is stretched one way and squashed the other. For any rotation it is cos^2 + sin^2 = 1. For a shear it is also 1: the parallelogram has the same area as the square. For a reflection it is -1: same area, but orientation flipped. A negative determinant is a quick test that a transform mirrors the object.

A note on conventions: We use column vectors and write P' = M P, so the matrix is on the left. Some books, and older APIs, use row vectors and write P' = P M, with every matrix transposed. Both are correct; the results are identical as long as you are consistent. When reading a textbook, check which one it uses before copying a matrix.

Real life example 1, Google Maps on a phone: When you drag the map, the app applies a translation. Pinch to zoom applies scaling about your fingers' midpoint. Two-finger twist applies a rotation. Each gesture updates one 3 x 3 matrix, and every road, label and pin is drawn through that matrix. That is why the whole map moves together smoothly.

Real life example 2, a design for a T-shirt print in a Gazipur factory: A designer places a logo, scales it to fit the chest, rotates it slightly for style, and mirrors it for a heat transfer print that is applied face down. Each action is a transformation on the vector logo. The design software keeps the result as a matrix attached to the logo, so the original shape is never damaged and the actions can be undone.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that scaling and rotation are about the origin, so the object also moves. Writing the rotation matrix with the minus sign in the wrong place: for counterclockwise rotation with column vectors, the minus is on sin in the first row. Using degrees in a calculator set to radians. Forgetting the 1 in homogeneous coordinates. Thinking translation can be a 2 x 2 matrix.

What exams ask: Write the equations and homogeneous matrices for translation, scaling, rotation, reflection and shear. Derive the rotation equations from polar form. Transform a given point or triangle. Explain why homogeneous coordinates are needed. Give the inverse of each transform.

Recap: The basic 2D transformations are translation, scaling, rotation, reflection and shear. All except translation are linear 2 x 2 matrices; homogeneous coordinates (x, y, 1) turn all of them, translation included, into 3 x 3 matrices. Points are transformed by multiplying, and inverses undo each transform. Next lesson we combine several transforms into one matrix to rotate about any point, scale in place and reflect about any line.
key_points: A transformation maps every point (x, y) to a new point; we transform vertices and redraw the shape.
Translation: x' = x + tx, y' = y + ty; it is not linear, so it needs homogeneous coordinates.
Scaling about the origin: x' = sx x, y' = sy y; it also moves the object unless done about a fixed point.
Rotation by theta: x' = x cos - y sin, y' = x sin + y cos; rotating (3, 4) by 90 degrees gives (-4, 3).
Reflections: about x axis (x, -y), y axis (-x, y), origin (-x, -y), line y = x (y, x).
Shear in x: x' = x + shx y; it slants shapes into parallelograms.
Homogeneous coordinates write a point as (x, y, 1) so every 2D transform is a 3 x 3 matrix.
Inverses: T(-tx, -ty), S(1/sx, 1/sy), R(-theta), which equals the transpose of R(theta).
lessons.tip: Learn one fact deeply instead of memorising five matrices: the columns of a 2 x 2 matrix are where the unit vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1) end up. Rotate those two arrows in your head and you can rebuild any rotation, scaling, reflection or shear matrix.
lessons.task: On graph paper draw the triangle (1, 1), (4, 1), (1, 3). Apply, separately, a translation by (2, 3), a scaling by 2 about the origin, a 90 degree rotation, a reflection about y = x and an x shear with shx = 1. Draw each result in a different colour.

quiz.q: What is (3, 4) after a 90 degree counterclockwise rotation about the origin?
Why are homogeneous coordinates needed for 2D transformations?
options: To make translation a matrix multiplication like the others
quiz.explain: Translation is not linear, so it cannot be a 2 x 2 matrix; adding a third coordinate fixes that.

quiz.q: Reflecting (5, 2) about the line y = x gives:
quiz.explain: Reflection about y = x swaps the coordinates.

quiz.q: What is the inverse of the scaling S(2, 4)?
quiz.explain: The inverse of scaling uses the reciprocal factors 1/sx and 1/sy.

quiz.q: An x shear with shx = 2 maps the point (1, 1) to:
quiz.explain: x' = x + shx y = 1 + 2 = 3, and y stays 1.

lessons.title: Composite 2D Transformations: Pivots, Fixed Points and Order
lessons.content:
Think of a ceiling fan in your room. Its blades rotate, but not around the corner of the room; they rotate around the fan's own centre. If a computer only knows how to rotate around the origin (0, 0), how does it spin a fan drawn in the middle of the screen? The trick is a small dance of three steps: carry the fan to the origin, spin it there, and carry it back. Combining simple transforms like this is called composition, and it is how every real graphics program builds complex motion from the basic five.

What a composite transformation is: A composite transformation is a sequence of basic transformations applied one after another. With homogeneous coordinates each step is a 3 x 3 matrix, so the whole sequence can be multiplied into a single matrix. If we first apply M1, then M2, then M3, the point becomes P' = M3 (M2 (M1 P)) = (M3 M2 M1) P. The combined matrix is M = M3 M2 M1. Notice the order: the first transform applied is the rightmost in the product. This is the single most important rule in this lesson.

Why combine: Suppose a game has a character of 5,000 vertices and needs to apply 4 transforms every frame. Applying them one by one costs 4 matrix-vector products per vertex, 20,000 in total. Multiplying the 4 matrices first costs only 3 matrix-matrix products, done once, and then a single matrix-vector product per vertex, 5,000 in total. For an affine 3 x 3 matrix, each vertex needs only 4 multiplications and 4 additions: x' = a x + b y + c and y' = d x + e y + f. That is why GPUs receive one combined matrix rather than a list of steps.

Combining the same kind: Some combinations are simple. Two translations add: T(t1) then T(t2) equals T(t1 + t2). Two rotations about the origin add their angles: R(30) then R(60) equals R(90). Two scalings multiply: S(2, 2) then S(3, 0.5) equals S(6, 1). You can verify each by multiplying the matrices; they are good warm-up exam questions.

Order matters: Matrix multiplication is not commutative, and neither are transforms in general. Take the point (1, 0). Translate by (5, 0), then rotate 90 degrees about the origin: (1, 0) goes to (6, 0), then to (0, 6). Now rotate first, then translate: (1, 0) goes to (0, 1), then to (5, 1). Two different answers, (0, 6) and (5, 1). The same steps in a different order give a different picture. Exceptions where order does not matter include two translations, two rotations, two scalings, and a rotation together with a uniform scaling.

Rotation about a pivot point: To rotate by theta about a pivot (xr, yr): first translate the pivot to the origin with T(-xr, -yr); rotate with R(theta); translate back with T(xr, yr). The composite matrix is M = T(xr, yr) R(theta) T(-xr, -yr). Multiplying it out gives the rows (cos, -sin, xr(1 - cos) + yr sin), (sin, cos, yr(1 - cos) - xr sin), (0, 0, 1). The upper-left 2 x 2 part is the ordinary rotation; the last column is the correction that keeps the pivot fixed.

Worked example, rotating a triangle about a vertex: Rotate the triangle A(2, 2), B(4, 2), C(3, 4) by 90 degrees about A. With cos 90 = 0, sin 90 = 1, xr = yr = 2: the last column is 2(1 - 0) + 2(1) = 4 and 2(1 - 0) - 2(1) = 0. So M has rows (0, -1, 4), (1, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1). Apply it: A(2, 2) gives (-2 + 4, 2) = (2, 2), unchanged as a pivot should be. B(4, 2) gives (-2 + 4, 4) = (2, 4). C(3, 4) gives (-4 + 4, 3) = (0, 3). Check B step by step: translate B by (-2, -2) to get (2, 0), rotate to get (0, 2), translate back to get (2, 4). Same answer.

Scaling about a fixed point: To scale an object in place, around its centre or any fixed point (xf, yf): translate the fixed point to the origin, scale, translate back. M = T(xf, yf) S(sx, sy) T(-xf, -yf), which has rows (sx, 0, xf(1 - sx)), (0, sy, yf(1 - sy)), (0, 0, 1). Worked example: the square from (2, 2) to (4, 4) scaled by 2 about its centre (3, 3). The last column is 3(1 - 2) = -3 for both. So (2, 2) goes to (4 - 3, 4 - 3) = (1, 1) and (4, 4) goes to (8 - 3, 8 - 3) = (5, 5). The square is now from (1, 1) to (5, 5): twice as big, still centred at (3, 3). Compare with the last lesson, where scaling about the origin pushed it out to (4, 4)-(8, 8).

Scaling in a direction that is not an axis: To stretch an object along a diagonal, say along the line at 45 degrees: rotate so that the desired direction lines up with the x axis, scale in x, then rotate back. M = R(45) S(s, 1) R(-45). This pattern, rotate into a convenient frame, do the simple thing, rotate back, appears again and again in graphics.

Reflection about an arbitrary line: The basic reflections are about the x axis, y axis, origin and y = x. To reflect about a general line y = m x + c, use the same pattern: translate the line so it passes through the origin, T(0, -c); rotate it onto the x axis, R(-theta) where theta = arctan(m); reflect about the x axis; rotate back, R(theta); translate back, T(0, c). That is five matrices: M = T(0, c) R(theta) Rx R(-theta) T(0, -c).

Worked example, reflection about y = x + 1: Here m = 1, so theta = 45 degrees, and c = 1. Multiplying the five matrices gives rows (0, 1, -1), (1, 0, 1), (0, 0, 1). In plain words, (x, y) goes to (y - 1, x + 1). Take the point (3, 1): it goes to (0, 4). Check: the midpoint of (3, 1) and (0, 4) is (1.5, 2.5), and 2.5 = 1.5 + 1, so the midpoint lies on the mirror line. The segment from (3, 1) to (0, 4) has direction (-3, 3), which is perpendicular to the line's direction (1, 1). Both checks pass. When c = 0, the same recipe reduces to the simple swap (y, x) for the line y = x.

General form of a composite: Any combination of translations, rotations, scalings, reflections and shears gives a matrix of the form with rows (a, b, c), (d, e, f), (0, 0, 1). The 2 x 2 block (a, b, d, e) holds all the rotation, scaling, reflection and shear, and the column (c, f) holds the net translation. If you know a transform is rigid, the 2 x 2 block is orthogonal: its rows are unit vectors and perpendicular to each other.

Why two rotations add, in one line: Multiply R(b) R(a). The top-left entry is cos b cos a - sin b sin a, which the angle sum formula says is cos(a + b). The other entries work out the same way to sin(a + b) and -sin(a + b). So R(b) R(a) = R(a + b), and because a + b = b + a, the order of two rotations about the same point does not matter. You can prove the translation and scaling rules the same way in two lines each.

Undoing a composite: The inverse of a product is the product of the inverses in reverse order: (M3 M2 M1)^-1 = M1^-1 M2^-1 M3^-1. That matches common sense: to undo putting on socks and then shoes, you take off the shoes first. For rotation about a pivot, the inverse is T(xr, yr) R(-theta) T(-xr, -yr), the same recipe with the angle negated. Programs use this to turn a mouse click on the screen back into the object's own coordinates, for example to decide which rotated button you tapped.

Hierarchies of transforms: Real scenes are built in layers. A car has a body, and each wheel is attached to the body. The wheel has its own local matrix W, a rotation about its axle placed at its mounting point, and the body has a matrix B that places the whole car on the road. The final matrix for a wheel is B W: first spin the wheel in car coordinates, then move it with the car. Move the car and the wheels follow automatically. This parent-child chain of matrices is called a scene graph or transform hierarchy, and every game engine and animation tool uses it.

Row vectors and the order trap: If a book uses row vectors, P' = P M, the composite for first M1, then M2, then M3 is M = M1 M2 M3, written left to right. Same transforms, reversed order in the product, every matrix transposed. Students often mix the two conventions in one answer and get the order wrong. State your convention at the start of the answer and stick to it.

Real life example 1, a ceiling fan or a wall clock in an animated app: A clock app on your phone shows hands rotating about the clock's centre, not about the screen corner. Each hand has its own composite matrix: T(centre) R(angle) T(-centre). The minute hand's angle grows by 6 degrees every minute, the hour hand's by 0.5 degrees. Only the angle changes each frame; the recipe stays the same.

Real life example 2, a bus moving along a road on a transport app: In a Dhaka bus-tracking app, a small bus icon must turn to face the direction of the road and move along it. For each new GPS point, the app rotates the icon about its own centre to the road's heading, then translates it to the new position: M = T(position) R(heading) T(-iconCentre). If the order were wrong, the bus would swing around the map's origin like a hammer thrower.

Common mistakes: Multiplying matrices in the order the steps are listed, instead of reversed. Forgetting the translate-back step, so the object ends up near the origin. Using arctan(m) in degrees when the matrices expect radians. Assuming rotation and non-uniform scaling commute. And forgetting that the pivot or fixed point must map to itself; always check it.

What exams ask: Derive the composite matrix for rotation about a pivot or scaling about a fixed point. Rotate or scale a given triangle about a given point. Show that the order of transforms matters with an example. Derive the reflection matrix about y = x or about a general line y = m x + c. Show that two successive rotations add.

Recap: Composite transformations multiply basic matrices into one, with the first transform on the right: M = M3 M2 M1. Rotation about a pivot and scaling about a fixed point both follow the translate, transform, translate back pattern. Reflection about any line adds rotation steps to the same pattern. Order matters except in a few special cases. Next we use transformations to map a part of the world onto a part of the screen: windowing and viewports.
key_points: A composite transform multiplies basic matrices into one: first M1, then M2, then M3 gives M = M3 M2 M1.
Combining matrices once saves work: each vertex then needs only one matrix-vector product.
Two translations add, two rotations add angles, two scalings multiply.
Order matters in general: translate then rotate differs from rotate then translate.
Rotation about a pivot: M = T(xr, yr) R(theta) T(-xr, -yr).
Scaling about a fixed point: M = T(xf, yf) S(sx, sy) T(-xf, -yf); the fixed point does not move.
Reflection about y = m x + c: translate, rotate the line onto the x axis, reflect, rotate back, translate back.
Reflection about y = x + 1 maps (x, y) to (y - 1, x + 1), e.g. (3, 1) to (0, 4).
lessons.tip: After computing any composite matrix, test it on one special point you know the answer for: the pivot must stay fixed, a point on a mirror line must stay on it. This five-second check catches almost every order mistake.
lessons.task: Write the composite matrix that rotates by 90 degrees about (3, 2). Apply it to the square (3, 2), (5, 2), (5, 4), (3, 4) and draw before and after on graph paper. Then reverse the order of the three matrices, apply it again, and see what goes wrong.

quiz.q: To apply M1 first, then M2, then M3 to a column vector, the combined matrix is:
quiz.explain: With P' = M P, the first transform applied is the rightmost factor.

quiz.q: Rotating (1, 0) by 90 degrees about the origin and then translating by (5, 0) gives:
quiz.explain: Rotation gives (0, 1), then translation gives (5, 1).

quiz.q: Which matrix rotates about the pivot (xr, yr)?
quiz.explain: Move the pivot to the origin, rotate, then move it back; the first step is on the right.

quiz.q: Scaling the square (2,2)-(4,4) by 2 about its centre (3, 3) gives which corners?
quiz.explain: The translation part is 3(1 - 2) = -3, so (2,2) goes to (1,1) and (4,4) to (5,5).

quiz.q: Which pair of transforms always commutes?
options: A rotation and a non-uniform scaling
quiz.explain: Rotations about the same point add their angles in either order.

lessons.title: Windowing and the Viewport: From World Coordinates to the Screen
lessons.content:
Stand at the window of a tall building in Motijheel and look out. The city is huge, but you only see the part framed by your window. Now take a photo of that view with your phone: the phone shows it in a small rectangle on its screen, maybe in a corner of a chat. Two rectangles are involved: the window, which chooses what part of the world you look at, and the display area, which chooses where on the screen it appears. In computer graphics these are called the window and the viewport, and the rule that maps one to the other is the subject of this lesson.

World coordinates: Objects in a scene are described in units that make sense for the problem, not in pixels. A building plan is in metres, a map of Bangladesh is in kilometres or degrees of latitude and longitude, a chart of rice prices is in taka and months. This coordinate system is called world coordinates. The world is effectively unlimited; our screen is a small grid of pixels. So we need a way to choose a part of the world and fit it onto part of the screen.

The window: The window is a rectangle in world coordinates that selects what we want to see, given by xwmin, xwmax, ywmin and ywmax. Everything inside the window will be shown; everything outside will be cut away, which is the job of clipping in the next lessons. Note that the word window here has nothing to do with the windows of an operating system; it is the area of the world being viewed.

The viewport: The viewport is a rectangle on the display device, given by xvmin, xvmax, yvmin and yvmax, where the contents of the window will be drawn. It might be the whole screen, or a small area, like the mini-map in the corner of a game. A screen can have several viewports at once, each showing a different window, as in a split-screen two-player game or a CAD program showing top, front and side views together.

The mapping idea: We want a point that sits, say, halfway across the window to appear halfway across the viewport, and a point a quarter of the way up the window to appear a quarter of the way up the viewport. In other words, relative positions are preserved. Writing that for x: (xv - xvmin) / (xvmax - xvmin) = (xw - xwmin) / (xwmax - xwmin). The same equation holds for y.

The window-to-viewport formula: Solving for xv and yv gives xv = xvmin + (xw - xwmin) sx and yv = yvmin + (yw - ywmin) sy, where the scale factors are sx = (xvmax - xvmin) / (xwmax - xwmin) and sy = (yvmax - yvmin) / (ywmax - ywmin). In words: find how far the point is from the window's corner, scale that distance, and add it to the viewport's corner.

Worked example 1: Let the window be x from 10 to 50 and y from 20 to 60, and the viewport be x from 100 to 300 and y from 200 to 400. Then sx = 200 / 40 = 5 and sy = 200 / 40 = 5. The world point (30, 40) maps to xv = 100 + (30 - 10) x 5 = 200 and yv = 200 + (40 - 20) x 5 = 300, so (200, 300). This point was in the middle of the window, and (200, 300) is exactly the middle of the viewport. The window corner (50, 60) maps to (100 + 40 x 5, 200 + 40 x 5) = (300, 400), the viewport's top-right corner, as expected.

As a composite matrix: The mapping is a translation, a scaling, and another translation, exactly the pattern of the last lesson. First move the window's corner to the origin with T(-xwmin, -ywmin), then scale with S(sx, sy), then move to the viewport's corner with T(xvmin, yvmin). The window-to-viewport matrix is M = T(xvmin, yvmin) S(sx, sy) T(-xwmin, -ywmin), with rows (sx, 0, xvmin - sx xwmin), (0, sy, yvmin - sy ywmin), (0, 0, 1). For our example the last column is 100 - 5 x 10 = 50 and 200 - 5 x 20 = 100, so xv = 5 xw + 50 and yv = 5 yw + 100. Check with (30, 40): 150 + 50 = 200 and 200 + 100 = 300. It matches.

Aspect ratio and distortion: If sx and sy are equal, shapes keep their proportions. If they differ, circles become ellipses and squares become rectangles. Example 2: window x from 0 to 100, y from 0 to 50 (a wide 2:1 area), viewport 400 x 400 pixels (a square). Then sx = 400 / 100 = 4 but sy = 400 / 50 = 8, so everything is stretched twice as much vertically. A round roundabout on a map would look like a tall oval. To avoid distortion, make the window and viewport have the same aspect ratio, or use the smaller scale factor for both and leave empty bars at the sides, which is what video players do with letterboxing.

Normalized device coordinates: Different devices have different resolutions: a 1920 x 1080 monitor, a 2400 x 1080 phone, an A4 printer. To keep programs device independent, many systems map the window first to a standard square, either from 0 to 1 or from -1 to 1 in each direction, called normalized device coordinates (NDC). Using the 0 to 1 version, our point (30, 40) becomes ((30 - 10) / 40, (40 - 20) / 40) = (0.5, 0.5). Then a final workstation transformation maps NDC to the actual device's pixels. OpenGL uses NDC from -1 to 1, and you will meet it again in the 3D pipeline.

The flipped y axis: Many screens put (0, 0) at the top-left with y growing downward, while world coordinates usually have y growing upward. The mapping then flips y: yv = yvmax - (yw - ywmin) sy. For a viewport from y = 0 to 480 on such a screen, a world point at the bottom of the window lands at row 480 and one at the top lands at row 0. Forgetting this is the classic reason students see their first graph upside down.

A y-flip worked example: Keep the window x 10 to 50, y 20 to 60, and the viewport x 100 to 300, rows 200 to 400, but on a screen where rows grow downward. The world point (30, 55) is near the top of the window. With the flipped formula, yv = 400 - (55 - 20) x 5 = 400 - 175 = 225, a row near the top of the viewport. Without the flip we would get 200 + 175 = 375, near the bottom: the picture would be upside down. The x formula is unchanged, so xv = 200.

The inverse mapping: Sometimes we need to go the other way, from a pixel back to the world, for example when the user taps the screen to drop a pin on a map. Just solve the formula backwards: xw = xwmin + (xv - xvmin) / sx, yw = ywmin + (yv - yvmin) / sy, or multiply by the inverse matrix. A tap at pixel (250, 350) in our first example corresponds to world (10 + 150/5, 20 + 150/5) = (40, 50). This inverse is how every touch on a map, chart or game board is turned into a position the program understands.

Zooming and panning: Because the viewport is fixed on the screen, changing the window changes what we see. Make the window smaller and the same viewport shows less of the world, so objects look bigger: zoom in. Make it larger: zoom out. Move the window without changing its size: pan. For example, halving the window from 40 x 40 to 20 x 20 world units doubles sx and sy from 5 to 10. Map apps do exactly this when you pinch or drag. Changing the viewport instead, while keeping the window, moves or resizes the picture on screen without changing its content.

The 2D viewing pipeline: Putting it together, a 2D drawing passes through these coordinate systems. Modelling coordinates: each object is defined in its own convenient frame, like a car icon centred at (0, 0). Modelling transformations place it into world coordinates. A viewing transformation may rotate the window, giving viewing coordinates, for example when a navigation app turns the map so your direction of travel points up. Then the window-to-viewport mapping, usually via normalized coordinates, and finally device coordinates in pixels. Clipping is done against the window, or the unit square in normalized coordinates, before rasterization, so that only visible parts are drawn.

Why clipping fits here: Objects partly outside the window would map outside the viewport, possibly onto other viewports or off the screen. Drawing them would waste time and could even overwrite other parts of the display. So before or during the mapping, every line and polygon is cut to the window's boundary. The next three lessons are about doing that efficiently: Cohen-Sutherland, Liang-Barsky and Sutherland-Hodgman.

Real life example 1, a ride-sharing map: Pathao or Uber shows Dhaka's streets. The world coordinates are map positions in metres. The window is the part of the city around you, maybe 2 km wide. The viewport is the map area of your phone screen, leaving room for buttons. When the driver gets closer, the app may shrink the window to zoom in on both of you, and the same window-to-viewport formula positions every street and car icon.

Real life example 2, a sales chart in a shop's accounting software: A shop owner in Chattogram views monthly sales. World x runs from month 1 to 12, world y from 0 to 5,00,000 taka. The chart's viewport is a 600 x 300 pixel box on the screen. The program uses sx = 600 / 11 and sy = 300 / 500000 and flips y because screen rows grow downward. If she changes the y range to 0 to 2,00,000 taka to see small months better, the window shrinks vertically and the bars grow taller: a vertical zoom.

Common mistakes: Using the viewport size divided by the window size the wrong way round. Forgetting to subtract xwmin before scaling. Ignoring the y flip on devices where y grows downward. Choosing a window and viewport with different aspect ratios and getting unwanted distortion. Confusing the graphics window with an operating system window.

What exams ask: Define window, viewport, world coordinates and normalized device coordinates. Derive the window-to-viewport transformation and write it as a composite matrix. Map a given point for given window and viewport. Explain zooming and panning. Draw and explain the 2D viewing pipeline.

Recap: The window selects what part of the world to see; the viewport selects where it appears on the screen. The mapping keeps relative positions: xv = xvmin + (xw - xwmin) sx, with sx = viewport width / window width, and similarly for y. As a matrix it is translate, scale, translate. Equal scale factors avoid distortion; changing the window zooms and pans. Before mapping, everything outside the window must be clipped, which is our next topic.
key_points: World coordinates use the problem's own units; the window is a rectangle in world coordinates that selects what to show.
The viewport is a rectangle on the screen where the window's contents are drawn; a screen may have several viewports.
xv = xvmin + (xw - xwmin) sx and yv = yvmin + (yw - ywmin) sy, with sx and sy = viewport size / window size.
The mapping matrix is T(xvmin, yvmin) S(sx, sy) T(-xwmin, -ywmin).
Different sx and sy distort shapes; matching aspect ratios avoids it.
Normalized device coordinates (0..1 or -1..1) make programs device independent.
Shrinking the window zooms in, enlarging zooms out, moving it pans.
lessons.tip: Always sanity-check a window-to-viewport answer with the window's centre and corners: the centre must land on the viewport's centre and the corners on its corners.
lessons.task: Choose a window of x 0 to 12 (months) and y 0 to 100 (marks), and a viewport of 600 x 300 pixels starting at (50, 50) on a screen where y grows downward. Map the points (3, 40), (6, 75) and (12, 100), and check them by sketching the chart.

quiz.q: What does the window select in 2D viewing?
options: Where on the screen the picture appears
Which part of the world is shown
quiz.explain: The window is a rectangle in world coordinates choosing what to display; the viewport chooses where.

quiz.q: Window x 10..50, y 20..60 and viewport x 100..300, y 200..400. Where does (30, 40) map?
Which matrix maps window to viewport?
quiz.explain: Move the window corner to the origin, scale, then move to the viewport corner.

quiz.q: If sx is not equal to sy, what happens to a circle?
quiz.explain: Different scale factors stretch one direction more, distorting shapes.

quiz.q: With the viewport fixed, making the window smaller causes:
quiz.explain: Less of the world fills the same screen area, so objects look larger.

lessons.title: Line Clipping with Cohen-Sutherland Region Codes
lessons.content:
Imagine you cut out a photo of a cricket match to paste into a scrapbook frame. You place a rectangular frame over the photo and trim away everything outside it with scissors. Some players are fully inside the frame and stay, some are fully outside and are thrown away, and some are cut in half by the frame's edge. Clipping in computer graphics is exactly that trimming: keep the parts of lines and shapes that lie inside the window, and cut off the rest. This lesson covers the most famous line clipping method, the Cohen-Sutherland algorithm, with a full worked example.

What clipping is and why we need it: A clipping algorithm decides which parts of a picture lie inside a region, called the clip window, and removes everything outside. In 2D viewing the clip window is usually the window rectangle from the last lesson, given by xmin, xmax, ymin and ymax. Without clipping, parts of objects outside the window would be mapped outside the viewport, wasting time, drawing over other parts of the screen, or even producing coordinates too large for the hardware. Clipping happens for every frame and every object, so it must be fast.

Point clipping: The simplest case is a single point (x, y). It is kept if xmin <= x <= xmax and ymin <= y <= ymax; otherwise it is discarded. Four comparisons. For example, with the window x from 10 to 50 and y from 10 to 40, the point (30, 20) is kept and the point (60, 20) is discarded because 60 > 50. Point clipping is used for things like particles in a game, rain drops or stars.

Line clipping, three cases: A line segment from P1 to P2 relative to the window can be completely inside (keep it all), completely outside (throw it away), or partially inside (keep only the inside piece, computing new end points on the window's boundary). Checking whether both end points are inside is easy. The hard part is to recognise quickly the lines that are completely outside, and to find intersection points efficiently for the rest. Computing intersections is expensive compared with comparisons, so a good algorithm avoids them whenever it can.

The nine regions: The four lines x = xmin, x = xmax, y = ymin and y = ymax extend infinitely and divide the plane into nine regions: the window in the centre, and eight regions around it: left, right, top, bottom and the four corners. Cohen and Sutherland's idea, from around 1967, was to give each region a 4-bit code, so that the position of a point relative to the window can be described with four bits and compared with fast bitwise operations.

Region codes: Each end point gets a 4-bit outcode, usually written in the order T B R L (top, bottom, right, left). Bit L is 1 if x < xmin. Bit R is 1 if x > xmax. Bit B is 1 if y < ymin. Bit T is 1 if y > ymax. A point inside the window has code 0000. A point to the left only has 0001. A point above and to the right has 1010. A point below and to the left has 0101. Because a point cannot be both left and right, or both above and below, at most two bits are ever set.

Computing a code: For the window x from 10 to 50 and y from 10 to 40: the point (0, 20) has x < 10, so L = 1, and y is in range, so its code is 0001. The point (60, 50) has x > 50 and y > 40, so R = 1 and T = 1: code 1010. The point (30, 25) is inside: 0000. Each code needs at most four comparisons, the same as point clipping.

Trivial accept: If both end points have code 0000, the whole line is inside, because the window is convex. We draw it without any intersection calculation. In bitwise terms: if (code1 OR code2) == 0000, accept. The line from (20, 20) to (30, 30) is accepted immediately.

Trivial reject: If both end points are on the same outside side of the window, for example both to the left, the whole line is outside. In bitwise terms: if (code1 AND code2) != 0000, reject. The AND has a 1 bit exactly when both points share an outside side. Example: (0, 0) has code 0101 (left and bottom) and (5, 50) has code 1001 (left and top). The AND is 0001, not zero, so the line is rejected without computing anything: both points are left of x = 10, so the whole segment is.

The remaining case: If the OR is not zero but the AND is zero, the line may cross the window or may pass outside near a corner. We cannot decide yet. So we pick an end point that is outside (one with a non-zero code), pick one of its set bits, and cut the line at the corresponding boundary. The outside piece is thrown away, the end point is replaced by the intersection, its code is recomputed, and we test again for trivial accept or reject. The loop repeats until the line is accepted or rejected. At most four cuts are ever needed.

Intersection formulas: With the line through (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) and slope m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1): at a vertical boundary x = xmin or x = xmax, y = y1 + m (x - x1). At a horizontal boundary y = ymin or y = ymax, x = x1 + (y - y1) / m. For a vertical line, x2 = x1, only the horizontal boundaries can be crossed and the x stays the same, so no division by zero happens if you only use the formula for the bit that is actually set.

Worked example, full trace: Window x from 10 to 50, y from 10 to 40. Line P1(0, 20) to P2(60, 50). Codes: P1 = 0001 (left), P2 = 1010 (top and right). OR = 1011, not zero, so not accepted. AND = 0000, so not rejected. Slope m = 30 / 60 = 0.5. Step 1: P1 is outside with bit L. Cut at x = 10: y = 20 + 0.5 x (10 - 0) = 25. New P1 = (10, 25), code 0000. Test again: OR = 1010, AND = 0000. Step 2: P2 is outside; check its bits in the order L, R, B, T and take R first. Cut at x = 50: y = 20 + 0.5 x (50 - 0) = 45. New P2 = (50, 45), code 1000 (still above). Test again: OR = 1000, AND = 0000. Step 3: P2 has bit T. Cut at y = 40: x = 0 + (40 - 20) / 0.5 = 40. New P2 = (40, 40), code 0000. Now OR = 0000: accept. The visible part is from (10, 25) to (40, 40).

Worked example, a corner miss: Same window, line from (0, 35) to (20, 50). Codes: 0001 and 1000. AND = 0000, so it is not trivially rejected, even though the line actually passes above the window's top-left corner. Cut at x = 10: the slope is 15 / 20 = 0.75, so y = 35 + 0.75 x 10 = 42.5, new point (10, 42.5) with code 1000. Now both codes are 1000, AND = 1000, so the line is rejected. This example shows why the loop is needed: one cut revealed that the rest of the line is outside.

The algorithm in pseudo-code: c1 = code(P1); c2 = code(P2); loop: if (c1 | c2) == 0: accept and draw; stop. if (c1 & c2) != 0: reject; stop. c = c1 if c1 != 0 else c2; compute the intersection (x, y) with the boundary of one set bit of c; if c == c1: P1 = (x, y); c1 = code(P1) else: P2 = (x, y); c2 = code(P2).

Strengths and weaknesses: Cohen-Sutherland is very fast when most lines are either fully inside or fully outside, which is common when the window is very large (most lines are inside) or very small (most lines are outside), because the bitwise tests settle them instantly. Its weakness is lines that need several cuts: it may compute intersections that are later thrown away, like the cut at (50, 45) in our example, which was outside and immediately cut again. It also uses division and floating point for each intersection. The next lesson's Liang-Barsky algorithm reduces this wasted work.

Clipping in 3D: The same idea extends to 3D with a 6-bit code for a box-shaped view volume (left, right, bottom, top, near, far). Real GPU pipelines clip against the view volume in homogeneous coordinates, which we will meet in the 3D viewing lesson. The bitwise accept and reject idea, often called outcodes, is still used to discard whole objects cheaply.

Real life example 1, a map app: When you zoom into Dhanmondi on a map, thousands of road segments of the whole of Dhaka are still in memory. Most are completely outside the visible window and are rejected with one AND operation; roads fully on screen are accepted with one OR; only roads crossing the screen's edge need intersection calculations. That is why panning feels smooth even with huge maps.

Real life example 2, a game's mini-map: A strategy game shows a small mini-map in the corner of the screen with unit paths as lines. The mini-map's viewport must not draw over the main game view, so every path line is clipped to the mini-map's window first. Without clipping, a long path would be drawn right across the main battlefield.

Common mistakes: Getting the region code bits wrong, especially mixing up top and bottom when the screen's y points down. Using OR for rejection and AND for acceptance instead of the other way round. Thinking that AND = 0000 means the line must cross the window; it may still miss a corner. Forgetting to recompute the code after replacing an end point. Using the wrong slope formula for horizontal boundaries.

What exams ask: Explain region codes with a diagram of nine regions. State trivial accept and reject conditions. Clip a given line against a given window step by step, showing codes and intersection points at each step. Discuss advantages and disadvantages, and compare with Liang-Barsky.

Recap: Cohen-Sutherland assigns each end point a 4-bit region code TBRL. If OR is zero the line is inside; if AND is non-zero it is outside. Otherwise an outside end point is moved to the intersection with one boundary, its code is recomputed, and the tests repeat. For the window 10..50 by 10..40, the line (0, 20)-(60, 50) is clipped to (10, 25)-(40, 40). Next lesson: a parametric approach that finds the visible piece with fewer wasted calculations.
key_points: Clipping keeps only the parts of a picture inside the clip window; point clipping needs four comparisons.
Cohen-Sutherland divides the plane into nine regions and gives each end point a 4-bit code in the order T B R L.
A bit is 1 when the point is above ymax (T), below ymin (B), right of xmax (R) or left of xmin (L); inside is 0000.
Trivial accept: code1 OR code2 == 0000; trivial reject: code1 AND code2 != 0000.
Otherwise move an outside end point to its intersection with a boundary, recompute its code and test again.
Intersections: y = y1 + m (x - x1) at vertical boundaries, x = x1 + (y - y1)/m at horizontal boundaries.
It is fastest when most lines are fully inside or outside, but may compute intersections that are later discarded.
lessons.tip: Draw the nine-region diagram with its codes in a corner of every clipping answer. It takes ten seconds, earns marks, and stops you from mixing up the bit order.
lessons.task: Using the window x 10 to 50, y 10 to 40, compute region codes for the lines (5, 5)-(60, 30), (20, 45)-(40, 50) and (30, 0)-(30, 60). Decide accept, reject or clip for each, and clip the ones that need it step by step.

quiz.q: In Cohen-Sutherland, when is a line trivially rejected?
options: When code1 AND code2 is not 0000
quiz.explain: A non-zero AND means both end points share an outside side, so the whole line is outside.

quiz.q: For the window x 10..50, y 10..40, what is the code (TBRL) of (60, 50)?
quiz.explain: x > 50 sets R and y > 40 sets T, giving 1010.

quiz.q: If both end points have code 0000, the line is:
quiz.explain: The window is convex, so a segment with both ends inside lies entirely inside.

quiz.q: Clipping (0, 20)-(60, 50) against the left boundary x = 10 gives which point?
The line (0, 35)-(20, 50) has codes 0001 and 1000. What is the final result?
options: Clipped to a short visible piece
quiz.explain: Cutting at x = 10 gives (10, 42.5) with code 1000; then the AND is 1000, so the line is rejected.

lessons.title: Liang-Barsky Line Clipping: The Parametric Way
lessons.content:
Imagine a train running from Dhaka to Chattogram, and a section of track where the railway allows filming for a TV drama. The film crew does not care about the whole journey; they only want to know at what fraction of the trip the train enters the filming zone and at what fraction it leaves. If the train enters at 30 percent of the journey and leaves at 45 percent, the visible part is between those two moments. Liang-Barsky clipping thinks about a line in exactly this way: as a journey from one end point to the other, measured by a parameter u from 0 to 1, and it finds the moment of entering and the moment of leaving the window.

Why another algorithm: Cohen-Sutherland is simple, but for lines that cross the window it may compute intersection points that are later thrown away, and it loops, recomputing region codes. In 1984 You-Dong Liang and Brian Barsky published a method that does all its decisions with simple comparisons of ratios and computes the actual clipped end points only once, at the very end. It is based on the parametric form of a line, an idea that Cyrus and Beck had used earlier (1978) for clipping against any convex polygon.

The parametric line: A segment from P0(x0, y0) to P1(x1, y1) can be written as x = x0 + u dx and y = y0 + u dy, where dx = x1 - x0, dy = y1 - y0 and u runs from 0 to 1. At u = 0 we are at P0, at u = 1 at P1, at u = 0.5 at the midpoint. Every point of the segment has its own u value, like the fraction of the train journey. Clipping then becomes: find the range of u for which the point is inside the window.

The four inequalities: A point is inside the window when xmin <= x <= xmax and ymin <= y <= ymax. Substituting the parametric form gives four inequalities: xmin <= x0 + u dx, x0 + u dx <= xmax, ymin <= y0 + u dy, and y0 + u dy <= ymax. Each can be rearranged into the same shape: u pk <= qk, for k = 1, 2, 3, 4.

The p and q values: Left boundary: p1 = -dx, q1 = x0 - xmin. Right boundary: p2 = dx, q2 = xmax - x0. Bottom boundary: p3 = -dy, q3 = y0 - ymin. Top boundary: p4 = dy, q4 = ymax - y0. Memorise the pattern: p alternates minus and plus the change, and q is the distance from the start point to that boundary measured toward the inside. Each q is positive when P0 is on the inside of that boundary.

The meaning of pk: If pk = 0, the line is parallel to that boundary. Then if qk < 0 the line lies completely outside that boundary and can be rejected at once; if qk >= 0 that boundary does not cut the line and can be ignored. If pk < 0, the line goes from the outside to the inside of that boundary as u increases: it is entering. If pk > 0, the line goes from inside to outside: it is leaving. In both non-zero cases the crossing happens at u = rk = qk / pk.

Entering and leaving: Start with u1 = 0 and u2 = 1, the whole segment. For each boundary where pk < 0 (entering), set u1 = max(u1, rk): the line cannot be inside before it has entered through every boundary. For each boundary where pk > 0 (leaving), set u2 = min(u2, rk): the line must be finished before it leaves through any boundary. At the end, if u1 > u2, the line is completely outside and is rejected. Otherwise the visible part runs from u1 to u2, and only now do we compute the two end points.

Worked example 1: Window x from 10 to 50, y from 10 to 40, the same as the last lesson. Line from (0, 20) to (60, 50), so dx = 60 and dy = 30. Left: p1 = -60, q1 = 0 - 10 = -10, r1 = -10 / -60 = 1/6, entering. Right: p2 = 60, q2 = 50 - 0 = 50, r2 = 50 / 60 = 5/6, leaving. Bottom: p3 = -30, q3 = 20 - 10 = 10, r3 = 10 / -30 = -1/3, entering. Top: p4 = 30, q4 = 40 - 20 = 20, r4 = 20 / 30 = 2/3, leaving.

Finishing example 1: u1 = max(0, 1/6, -1/3) = 1/6. u2 = min(1, 5/6, 2/3) = 2/3. Since 1/6 < 2/3, the line is visible from u = 1/6 to u = 2/3. Start point: x = 0 + (1/6)(60) = 10, y = 20 + (1/6)(30) = 25, so (10, 25). End point: x = 0 + (2/3)(60) = 40, y = 20 + (2/3)(30) = 40, so (40, 40). Exactly the same answer as Cohen-Sutherland, (10, 25) to (40, 40), but we computed only two points, not three, and no region codes.

Worked example 2, a rejected line: Same window, line (0, 35) to (20, 50), so dx = 20, dy = 15. Left: p1 = -20, q1 = -10, r1 = 0.5, entering. Right: p2 = 20, q2 = 50, r2 = 2.5, leaving. Bottom: p3 = -15, q3 = 25, r3 = -5/3, entering. Top: p4 = 15, q4 = 40 - 35 = 5, r4 = 1/3, leaving. So u1 = max(0, 0.5, -5/3) = 0.5 and u2 = min(1, 2.5, 1/3) = 1/3. Now u1 = 0.5 > u2 = 0.333: the line leaves through the top before it has entered through the left. Rejected, with no intersection points computed at all.

Worked example 3, a parallel line: Take the horizontal line from (20, 5) to (40, 5), below the window. dy = 0, so p3 = p4 = 0. q3 = y0 - ymin = 5 - 10 = -5, which is negative: the line is parallel to the bottom boundary and on its outside. Reject immediately. If instead the line were at y = 25, q3 = 15 and q4 = 15 would both be non-negative, so those boundaries are ignored and only the left and right boundaries decide.

Why the max and min make sense: Think of the window as the overlap of four half-planes: right of the left edge, left of the right edge, above the bottom, below the top. To be inside, a point must be inside all four at once. Each entering boundary says you are not inside me until u reaches rk, so the latest entering time wins. Each leaving boundary says you are inside me only until u reaches rk, so the earliest leaving time wins. If the latest entry comes after the earliest exit, there is no moment when the line is inside all four.

The algorithm in pseudo-code: dx = x1 - x0; dy = y1 - y0; p = [-dx, dx, -dy, dy]; q = [x0 - xmin, xmax - x0, y0 - ymin, ymax - y0]; u1 = 0; u2 = 1; for k in 1..4: if p[k] == 0: if q[k] < 0: reject; else: r = q[k] / p[k]; if p[k] < 0: u1 = max(u1, r) else: u2 = min(u2, r); if u1 > u2: reject; else draw from (x0 + u1 dx, y0 + u1 dy) to (x0 + u2 dx, y0 + u2 dy). Many implementations also reject early inside the loop as soon as u1 > u2.

Comparing with Cohen-Sutherland: Liang-Barsky needs at most four divisions for the r values and computes the final end points once, so it usually does less work for lines that need clipping. Cohen-Sutherland can be faster when nearly all lines are trivially accepted or rejected, because a single bitwise test settles them. Liang-Barsky also extends neatly to 3D with six inequalities for a box view volume. In exams, the usual conclusion is that Liang-Barsky is more efficient in general because it avoids computing unnecessary intersections.

Extending to 3D: For a box-shaped view volume with near and far planes, add z = z0 + u dz and two more inequalities: p5 = -dz, q5 = z0 - zmin and p6 = dz, q6 = zmax - z0. The rest of the algorithm does not change at all: six r values instead of four, the same max for entering and min for leaving. This is one reason parametric clipping is popular in 3D pipelines, where every triangle edge must be tested against six planes.

Cyrus-Beck in one paragraph: Cyrus and Beck's method clips a line against any convex polygon. For each polygon edge, with an inward normal vector N and a point E on the edge, the crossing parameter is u = N.(P0 - E) / (-N.(P1 - P0)), and the sign of N.(P1 - P0) tells whether the line is entering or leaving. Taking the latest entry and earliest exit gives the visible range, just like Liang-Barsky. Liang-Barsky is in fact Cyrus-Beck specialised to an upright rectangle, where the normals are the axis directions and everything simplifies into the p and q values.

Real life example 1, CAD drawings of a building: An engineer in a Dhaka firm zooms into one floor of a 20-storey building plan. Thousands of wall lines cross the edges of the view. Using a parametric clipper, each crossing line is reduced to its visible piece with a few divisions, and the end points are computed once, keeping the drawing responsive while panning.

Real life example 2, laser show or plotter limits: A laser projector at a concert in Bangabandhu stadium can only steer its beam within a fixed rectangle. Any line in the show's design that goes beyond the limits must be clipped to the allowed area before being sent to the projector's mirrors. A parametric clipper is ideal because it outputs the visible part directly as start and end parameters along each line.

Common mistakes: Getting the signs of p wrong; check that p1 = -dx for the left boundary. Swapping max and min: entering uses max, leaving uses min. Forgetting to start u1 at 0 and u2 at 1, which would let the clipped piece extend beyond the original end points. Dividing by p when p = 0 instead of checking q. And computing the end points before all four boundaries have been processed.

What exams ask: Derive the four inequalities and the p and q values. Explain entering and leaving and the roles of u1 and u2. Clip a given line against a given window with a full table of p, q and r. Compare Liang-Barsky with Cohen-Sutherland. Write a short note on Cyrus-Beck.

Recap: Liang-Barsky writes the line as P0 + u (P1 - P0) and turns the window into four inequalities u pk <= qk. Negative pk means entering, update u1 = max(u1, qk/pk); positive pk means leaving, update u2 = min(u2, qk/pk); zero pk means parallel, reject if qk < 0. If u1 > u2 reject, otherwise compute the visible end points once. Next lesson: clipping whole polygons, where line clipping is not enough.
key_points: Liang-Barsky uses the parametric line x = x0 + u dx, y = y0 + u dy with u from 0 to 1.
The window becomes four inequalities u pk <= qk with p = (-dx, dx, -dy, dy) and q = (x0 - xmin, xmax - x0, y0 - ymin, ymax - y0).
pk = 0: line parallel to that boundary; reject if qk < 0, otherwise ignore that boundary.
pk < 0: entering, u1 = max(u1, qk/pk); pk > 0: leaving, u2 = min(u2, qk/pk).
If u1 > u2 the line is outside; otherwise the visible part is from u1 to u2.
End points are computed only once, so it avoids the wasted intersections of Cohen-Sutherland.
Cyrus-Beck generalises the same idea to any convex clip polygon using edge normals.
lessons.tip: Make a four-row table with columns boundary, p, q, r, entering or leaving. Fill it mechanically, then just read off the largest entering r and the smallest leaving r. The table is the whole algorithm.
lessons.task: With the window x 10 to 50, y 10 to 40, clip the lines (5, 5)-(60, 30) and (20, 0)-(30, 60) using Liang-Barsky with a full p, q, r table. Then clip the first one with Cohen-Sutherland and compare how many intersection points each method computed.

quiz.q: In Liang-Barsky, what does pk < 0 mean for that boundary?
options: The line is parallel to it
The line is leaving through it
The line is entering through it
quiz.explain: Negative pk means the line moves from outside to inside of that boundary as u increases.

quiz.q: What are p1 and q1 for the left boundary?
quiz.explain: From xmin <= x0 + u dx we get -u dx <= x0 - xmin.

quiz.q: When is a line rejected after processing all four boundaries?
quiz.explain: If the latest entry is after the earliest exit, the line is never inside all four half-planes.

quiz.q: For the line (0,20)-(60,50) and window 10..50 by 10..40, what is u2?
quiz.explain: Leaving values are 5/6 (right) and 2/3 (top); u2 = min(1, 5/6, 2/3) = 2/3.

quiz.q: A horizontal line y = 5 is clipped against ymin = 10. What happens?
options: It is rejected because p3 = 0 and q3 = -5 < 0
Division by zero stops the program
quiz.explain: dy = 0 makes p3 = 0; q3 = 5 - 10 < 0 means the line is outside the bottom boundary.

lessons.title: Polygon Clipping with Sutherland-Hodgman
lessons.content:
Think of a mango-shaped cut-out of coloured paper that you want to fit into a rectangular photo frame. If you only trimmed its outline as separate line pieces, you would be left with a few loose bits of edge, not a filled shape. What you actually want is a new, smaller paper shape that is the part of the mango lying inside the frame, with its own closed outline. That is polygon clipping: the result must still be a closed polygon that can be filled. This lesson explains why line clipping is not enough and how the Sutherland-Hodgman algorithm solves the problem in a beautifully simple way.

Why line clipping is not enough: Suppose we clip each edge of a filled triangle with Cohen-Sutherland or Liang-Barsky. We get the visible pieces of each edge, but where the triangle crosses the window boundary, the outline is broken: there is no edge along the window's border to close the shape. A scan-line filler given these pieces would not know where the inside is. Worse, if the window lies entirely inside a large polygon, every edge is outside and gets rejected, so we would draw nothing, even though the whole window should be filled. Polygon clipping must therefore output a closed list of vertices, including new vertices on the window border and pieces of the border itself.

The key idea, one edge at a time: Ivan Sutherland and Gary Hodgman (1974) noticed that clipping against a whole rectangle is hard, but clipping against a single infinite line is easy. A rectangular window is the intersection of four half-planes: right of the left edge, left of the right edge, above the bottom edge, below the top edge. So clip the polygon against the left boundary, producing a new polygon; clip that against the right boundary; then the bottom; then the top. After four passes, what remains is exactly the part inside the window. The same idea works for any convex clip window, with one pass per edge.

Inside and outside for one boundary: For the left boundary x = xmin, a point is inside if x >= xmin. For the right boundary, inside means x <= xmax. For the bottom, y >= ymin. For the top, y <= ymax. In each pass we only ask this one simple question, so each pass is just a loop over the polygon's edges.

The four cases: In one pass we walk around the polygon, looking at each edge from a start vertex S to an end vertex P, and decide what to output. Case 1, inside to inside: output P. Case 2, inside to outside: output only the intersection point I of the edge with the boundary. Case 3, outside to outside: output nothing. Case 4, outside to inside: output the intersection I and then P. Notice that every case outputs at most two points, and the outputs, taken in order, form the new polygon. Many students remember the rule as: output P whenever P is inside, and output I whenever the edge crosses the boundary, putting I first.

Computing the intersection: The intersection with a vertical boundary x = c is at y = yS + (c - xS)(yP - yS)/(xP - xS). With a horizontal boundary y = c it is at x = xS + (c - yS)(xP - xS)/(yP - yS). These are the same formulas used in Cohen-Sutherland. We only compute them when an edge actually crosses the boundary, so no division by zero occurs.

Worked example: Clip the triangle A(20, 20), B(40, 20), C(30, 60) against the window x from 10 to 50 and y from 10 to 40, the window of the last two lessons. The vertex list is A, B, C, and the edges are A to B, B to C and C to A.

Pass 1, left boundary x >= 10: all three vertices have x of at least 20, so all edges are inside to inside. Output: B, C, A, the same triangle, just starting from a different vertex. Pass 2, right boundary x <= 50: again all vertices are inside, so the triangle passes through unchanged. Pass 3, bottom boundary y >= 10: all y values are at least 20, unchanged again. Only one boundary actually cuts this triangle, which is common in practice; the passes that change nothing are cheap.

Pass 4, top boundary y <= 40: Vertex A(20, 20) is inside, B(40, 20) is inside, C(30, 60) is outside because 60 > 40. Edge A to B: inside to inside, output B(40, 20). Edge B to C: inside to outside, output only the intersection. Along B to C, y goes from 20 to 60, so y = 40 is halfway: x = 40 + 0.5 x (30 - 40) = 35, giving I1 = (35, 40). Edge C to A: outside to inside, output the intersection and then A. Along C to A, y goes from 60 to 20, so y = 40 is halfway again: x = 30 + 0.5 x (20 - 30) = 25, giving I2 = (25, 40); then output A(20, 20).

The result: The output list is (40, 20), (35, 40), (25, 40), (20, 20): a quadrilateral. The tip of the triangle above the window has been cut off and replaced by a new edge from (35, 40) to (25, 40) lying exactly along the window's top border. This new polygon is closed and can be filled with the scan-line algorithm. A triangle became a four-sided polygon; in general, clipping a convex polygon with n vertices against a rectangle can produce up to n + 4 vertices.

The algorithm in pseudo-code: function clipAgainst(polygon, boundary): output = empty list; S = last vertex of polygon; for each vertex P of polygon: if inside(P, boundary): if not inside(S, boundary): output.add(intersect(S, P, boundary)); output.add(P) else if inside(S, boundary): output.add(intersect(S, P, boundary)); S = P; return output. Then result = clipAgainst(clipAgainst(clipAgainst(clipAgainst(poly, left), right), bottom), top).
