lessons.task: Using N = (0, 0, 1), L = (0.6, 0, 0.8) and V = (0, 0.6, 0.8), compute N . L, R, R . V and the total Phong intensity with Ia = Il = 1, ka = 0.1, kd = 0.7, ks = 0.5 and n = 20. Then repeat with n = 2 and explain the difference.

quiz.q: According to Lambert's law, a light hitting a matte surface at 60 degrees from the normal gives what fraction of full diffuse brightness?
quiz.explain: Diffuse brightness is proportional to cos 60 = 0.5.

quiz.q: What does a large shininess exponent n produce?
quiz.explain: Raising R . V to a high power makes the highlight fall off quickly away from R.

quiz.q: Which formula gives the mirror reflection vector R?
quiz.explain: Reflecting L about N gives R = 2(N . L)N - L; (L + V)/|L + V| is the halfway vector.

quiz.q: Why is N . L clamped with max(0, N . L)?
options: Surfaces facing away from the light should get no diffuse light, not negative light
quiz.explain: A negative dot product means the light is behind the surface.

lessons.title: Shading Methods: Flat, Gouraud and Phong Shading
lessons.content:
Last lesson gave us a formula for how bright one point on a surface looks. But a 3D model of a football might have two thousand triangles, and each triangle covers hundreds of pixels on screen. Should we run the lighting formula once per triangle, once per corner, or once per pixel? That choice is called the shading method, and it decides whether the football looks like a faceted gem, a smooth ball with blurry highlights, or a smooth ball with crisp highlights. This lesson covers the three classic answers: flat shading, Gouraud shading and Phong shading, with a worked Gouraud example.

Illumination versus shading: Students often mix up these two words. The illumination model, like Phong's ambient plus diffuse plus specular, computes the colour at a single point given N, L and V. The shading method, also called a surface rendering method, decides where we evaluate that model and how we fill in the pixels between. Phong's name appears in both, which adds to the confusion: the Phong illumination model is the formula; Phong shading is the method of interpolating normals and applying a formula at every pixel. You can even use Phong shading with a different illumination model.

Polygon meshes approximate curves: A curved object like a ball is stored as a mesh of flat polygons, usually triangles. Each flat triangle has one geometric normal, perpendicular to its plane. But the real ball is curved, and its true normal changes smoothly from point to point. Shading methods differ in how hard they try to bring back that lost smoothness.

Flat shading: Also called constant shading. Compute the illumination once per polygon, using the polygon's normal, often at its centre or first vertex, and fill the entire polygon with that one colour. It is the fastest method: one lighting calculation per polygon. It is exactly right when the object really is made of flat faces, such as a cube or a building, and when the light and viewer are far away, so L and V are nearly constant across the face. On curved objects it shows every facet clearly, like a disco ball.

Vertex normals: To make a mesh look smooth, we need a normal at each vertex that represents the curved surface there, not any single face. The usual method averages the normals of all faces that share the vertex: N_v = (N1 + N2 + ... + Nk) / |N1 + N2 + ... + Nk|. For example, if two faces meeting at a vertex have normals (1, 0, 0) and (0, 1, 0), the vertex normal is (1, 1, 0) normalised, about (0.707, 0.707, 0): pointing halfway between. When the model is generated from a known shape, like a sphere, the exact normal can be used instead; for a sphere centred at the origin, the normal at a point is just the point divided by the radius.

Gouraud shading: Proposed by Henri Gouraud in 1971, it is also called intensity interpolation. Step 1: compute vertex normals. Step 2: apply the illumination model at each vertex, giving a vertex intensity or colour. Step 3: interpolate those intensities linearly along each edge of the polygon. Step 4: during scan conversion, interpolate between the left and right edge intensities across each scan line. Lighting is computed only three times per triangle, and everything else is cheap additions, the same incremental idea as DDA, scan-line fill and the z-buffer.

Gouraud worked example: Take a triangle with vertices A = (0, 0) with intensity 0.2, B = (10, 0) with intensity 0.8, and C = (0, 10) with intensity 0.6. Shade the pixel at (2, 5). Scan line y = 5 crosses edge AC at x = 0, halfway from A to C, so its intensity is 0.2 + 0.5 x (0.6 - 0.2) = 0.4. It crosses edge BC at x = 5, halfway from B to C, with intensity 0.8 + 0.5 x (0.6 - 0.8) = 0.7. Across the span from x = 0 to x = 5, intensity rises by (0.7 - 0.4) / 5 = 0.06 per pixel. At x = 2: 0.4 + 2 x 0.06 = 0.52. So each new pixel along the row just adds 0.06, and each new scan line adds a fixed step to each edge's intensity.

The interpolation formulas: Along an edge from vertex 1 to vertex 2, at scan line y, I_a = I1 + (I2 - I1)(y - y1)/(y2 - y1). Across the span, between the left value I_a at x_a and the right value I_b at x_b, I_p = I_a + (I_b - I_a)(x_p - x_a)/(x_b - x_a). In incremental form, moving one pixel right adds the constant delta I = (I_b - I_a)/(x_b - x_a). These two formulas are what exams expect you to write.

Gouraud in colour and with the z-buffer: For coloured objects the same interpolation is done three times, once each for red, green and blue, or once on a colour vector. It fits neatly into the scan-line loop we already have: as we walk along a span, we add one constant step to depth for the z-buffer and one constant step to each colour channel. So a hardware rasterizer can produce depth and Gouraud colour for every pixel using only additions, which is why early graphics cards could shade millions of pixels per second.

Strengths of Gouraud: It hides the facet edges of a curved mesh, because neighbouring triangles share vertex intensities, so colour is continuous across edges. It is cheap: lighting per vertex, not per pixel. That is why it was the standard real-time method for decades, built into early graphics hardware and the classic fixed-function OpenGL, and why it still suits low-power devices.

Weaknesses of Gouraud: Because lighting is computed only at vertices, a specular highlight that falls in the middle of a triangle can be missed completely: none of the three vertices sees it, so the interpolation never produces it. If a highlight falls exactly on a vertex, it is smeared over all the surrounding triangles, looking like a star-shaped blur, and it jumps or flickers as the object moves. Gouraud also shows Mach bands, described below, along edges where the intensity gradient changes.

Mach bands: The human visual system exaggerates sudden changes in brightness gradient. Where two regions meet with a change in slope, we see a slightly brighter or darker stripe that is not really there, named after the physicist Ernst Mach. Flat shading makes Mach bands very visible at every edge, because the intensity jumps. Gouraud removes the jumps but the slope still changes at edges, so faint bands remain. Phong shading reduces them further.

Phong shading: Proposed by Bui Tuong Phong in 1975 alongside his illumination model, it is also called normal-vector interpolation. Instead of interpolating intensities, interpolate the normal vectors themselves along edges and across scan lines, renormalise the interpolated normal at each pixel, and apply the full illumination model at every pixel. The interpolation formulas are the same as Gouraud's, but applied to each component of N rather than to I.

Why renormalise: Interpolating two unit vectors produces a vector shorter than unit length in between. For example, halfway between (1, 0, 0) and (0, 1, 0) is (0.5, 0.5, 0), with length about 0.707. Using it directly would make the middle of the polygon too dark, so we divide by its length, getting (0.707, 0.707, 0). This normalisation at every pixel is part of why Phong shading is more expensive.

Strengths and costs of Phong shading: Highlights appear in the right place and with the right shape, even in the middle of a large triangle, and move smoothly as the object or light moves. Curved surfaces look truly smooth, and Mach bands are greatly reduced. The cost is a full lighting calculation per pixel, typically several times more work than Gouraud. On modern GPUs this is routine: a fragment shader that receives an interpolated normal and computes lighting is per-pixel Phong shading, and nearly every 3D game today shades this way or with more advanced per-pixel models.

Smooth groups and hard edges: A real model usually mixes both kinds of surface. A rice cooker has a smooth curved body but a sharp rim where the lid meets it. If we average normals across the rim, the sharp edge looks soft and rubbery. So modelling tools let artists mark hard edges or smoothing groups: at those vertices the mesh stores separate normals for each side, so each side keeps its own face normal while curved parts are still averaged. A cube that should look sharp therefore stores 24 vertex normals, three at each corner, not 8.

Comparing the three: Flat shading computes lighting once per polygon, is fastest, and shows facets. Gouraud computes lighting per vertex and interpolates intensities, giving smooth diffuse shading but missing or smearing highlights. Phong interpolates normals and lights every pixel, giving accurate highlights at the highest cost. For a matte object with no highlights, Gouraud and Phong look almost the same; the difference shows on shiny objects.

Silhouettes stay polygonal: No shading method changes the geometry. The outline of a low-polygon ball is still a polygon, with straight segments, however smooth its interior looks. Fixing silhouettes needs more triangles or techniques like tessellation, not better shading. This is a favourite viva question.

Real life example 1, an old phone game versus a new one: Early 3D mobile games in the 2000s often used Gouraud shading because phones were slow; cars looked smooth but their shine looked blotchy. Today's games on a mid-range phone in Bangladesh compute lighting per pixel in fragment shaders, so a car's paint shows a sharp, moving reflection of the street lights.

Real life example 2, an architecture model: An architect showing a design for a new office in Motijheel uses flat shading for walls, floors and boxes, because they really are flat and flat shading makes each surface clearly distinct. For a curved glass facade on the same building, she switches to Phong shading so the sky's highlight slides naturally across the glass.

Common mistakes: Calling the Phong illumination model and Phong shading the same thing. Interpolating normals without renormalising. Saying Gouraud interpolates normals; it interpolates intensities. Thinking smooth shading fixes the polygonal outline. Forgetting that flat shading is the right choice for genuinely flat objects.

What exams ask: Distinguish illumination models from shading methods. Explain flat, Gouraud and Phong shading with steps and diagrams. Compute vertex normals by averaging. Calculate an interpolated intensity at a pixel in a triangle. Explain Mach bands. Compare Gouraud and Phong shading, especially regarding specular highlights and cost.

Recap: Flat shading lights each polygon once and shows facets. Gouraud shading averages face normals at vertices, lights the vertices, and interpolates intensities along edges and spans; our example gives 0.52 at (2, 5), with a step of 0.06 per pixel. It is cheap but can miss or smear highlights. Phong shading interpolates and renormalises normals and lights every pixel, giving correct highlights at higher cost, and is what modern fragment shaders do. Next we leave flat polygons behind and look at smooth curves: Bezier curves and B-splines.
key_points: The illumination model computes colour at a point; the shading method decides where to evaluate it and how to fill pixels.
Flat shading: one lighting calculation per polygon; fastest, correct for truly flat objects, faceted on curved ones.
Vertex normals are usually the normalised average of the normals of faces sharing the vertex.
Gouraud shading lights each vertex and linearly interpolates intensities along edges and across scan lines.
Gouraud example: edge values 0.4 and 0.7 on y = 5, step 0.06 per pixel, intensity 0.52 at (2, 5).
Gouraud can miss highlights inside a triangle or smear them around a vertex, and shows faint Mach bands.
Phong shading interpolates normals, renormalises them, and lights every pixel; highlights are accurate but cost is higher.
No shading method fixes a polygonal silhouette; that needs more geometry.
lessons.tip: Make a three-column table, flat, Gouraud, Phong, with rows for what is interpolated, how many lighting calculations per triangle, highlight quality, Mach bands and cost. Filling it from memory once is the best revision for this topic.
lessons.task: A triangle has vertices P = (0, 0) with intensity 0.1, Q = (8, 0) with intensity 0.9 and R = (0, 8) with intensity 0.5. Use Gouraud shading to find the intensity at pixel (3, 4). Then find the vertex normal at a vertex shared by faces with normals (0, 0, 1), (1, 0, 0) and (0, 1, 0).

quiz.q: What does Gouraud shading interpolate across a polygon?
quiz.explain: Gouraud lights the vertices and interpolates the resulting intensities.

quiz.q: On scan line y = 5, the left edge intensity is 0.4 at x = 0 and the right edge is 0.7 at x = 5. What is the intensity at x = 2?
Why does Phong shading renormalise interpolated normals?
options: Interpolated unit vectors are shorter than unit length
quiz.explain: The blend of two unit vectors is shorter, which would darken the lighting.

quiz.q: Which problem is typical of Gouraud shading?
options: Highlights inside a triangle can be missed
quiz.explain: Lighting is only computed at vertices, so a highlight between them never appears.

quiz.q: When is flat shading the most sensible choice?
options: For a shiny curved car body
For a smooth face in a film
For objects that really have flat faces, like boxes and walls
quiz.explain: Flat faces have one true normal, so flat shading is correct and fastest.

lessons.title: Curves: Parametric Curves, Bezier Curves and B-Splines
lessons.content:
Look at the Bangla letters on a shop sign, the curve of a car's bonnet, or the logo of a mobile operator. None of these shapes are made of straight lines or perfect circles. Designers draw them by placing a few control points and letting the computer bend a smooth curve through or near them. Every font on your phone, every vector drawing in Illustrator or Inkscape, and every car body designed in CAD uses this idea. This lesson explains how: parametric curves, continuity, Bezier curves with the de Casteljau algorithm worked step by step, and B-splines.

Why not y = f(x): An explicit equation like y = x^2 gives only one y for each x, so it cannot draw a loop, a vertical line, or the letter S lying on its side. An implicit equation like x^2 + y^2 = r^2 can describe a circle, but it is hard to draw points along it in order. Graphics therefore uses parametric curves: both coordinates are functions of a parameter t, P(t) = (x(t), y(t)), usually with t from 0 to 1. As t moves from 0 to 1, the point P(t) travels along the curve from start to end, like a rickshaw following a route. Loops, vertical tangents and 3D curves are all easy.

Interpolation versus approximation: A curve interpolates its control points if it passes through all of them. It approximates them if it is only pulled toward them, passing through some or none. Interpolating curves seem natural, but they often wiggle wildly between points. Approximating curves, like Bezier curves and B-splines, are smoother and more predictable, and designers quickly learn to steer them by moving control points.

Continuity: Long shapes are built from several curve segments joined end to end, so we care how smoothly they join. C0 continuity means the segments simply meet, with no gap, though there may be a sharp corner. C1 means the first derivatives, the tangent vectors, are equal at the join, so the direction and speed match and there is no corner. C2 means the second derivatives also match, so the curvature changes smoothly, which matters for car bodies and camera paths where a sudden change in curvature is visible or felt. G1, geometric continuity, means the tangent directions match but their lengths may differ: the curve looks smooth even if the parameter speed jumps.

The Bezier curve: Developed independently by Pierre Bezier at Renault and Paul de Casteljau at Citroen around 1960 for designing car bodies. A Bezier curve of degree n uses n + 1 control points P0 to Pn: P(t) = sum over k of B(k, n)(t) Pk, where B(k, n)(t) = C(n, k) t^k (1 - t)^(n - k) are the Bernstein polynomials. The most common is the cubic, n = 3, with four control points: P(t) = (1 - t)^3 P0 + 3t(1 - t)^2 P1 + 3t^2(1 - t) P2 + t^3 P3.

Properties of Bezier curves: The curve starts at P0 and ends at Pn; it passes through the end points but generally not the inner ones. The tangent at the start points from P0 toward P1, and at the end from Pn-1 toward Pn; for a cubic, P'(0) = 3(P1 - P0). The Bernstein weights are never negative and always sum to 1, so every point of the curve is a weighted average of the control points, and the whole curve lies inside the convex hull of the control points, a fact used for fast clipping and collision tests. Transforming the control points and then drawing gives the same result as drawing and then transforming, so to rotate a curve you just rotate its control points. The curve also never wiggles more than its control polygon, called the variation diminishing property.

Worked example, the formula: Let P0 = (0, 0), P1 = (1, 2), P2 = (3, 3), P3 = (4, 0). At t = 0.5 the Bernstein weights are (0.5)^3 = 0.125, 3 x 0.5 x 0.25 = 0.375, 0.375 and 0.125. So x = 0.125 x 0 + 0.375 x 1 + 0.375 x 3 + 0.125 x 4 = 2, and y = 0.125 x 0 + 0.375 x 2 + 0.375 x 3 + 0.125 x 0 = 1.875. The middle of the curve is (2, 1.875). Notice it does not reach P1 or P2, whose heights are 2 and 3: the curve is only pulled toward them.

The de Casteljau algorithm: The same point can be found by repeated linear interpolation, which is numerically stable and easy to draw by hand. Take the control polygon and, on each edge, find the point a fraction t along it. That gives one fewer point. Repeat on the new points until one point remains: that is P(t). Each step only uses lerp(A, B, t) = A + t(B - A).

de Casteljau worked: With the same points and t = 0.5. Level 1, midpoints of the three edges: between (0, 0) and (1, 2) is (0.5, 1); between (1, 2) and (3, 3) is (2, 2.5); between (3, 3) and (4, 0) is (3.5, 1.5). Level 2, midpoints of these: between (0.5, 1) and (2, 2.5) is (1.25, 1.75); between (2, 2.5) and (3.5, 1.5) is (2.75, 2). Level 3: between (1.25, 1.75) and (2.75, 2) is (2, 1.875). Exactly the same as the formula. As a bonus, the points along the left side of this triangle, P0, (0.5, 1), (1.25, 1.75) and (2, 1.875), are the control points of the left half of the curve, and the right side gives the right half. Splitting a curve this way is called subdivision.

Quadratic Bezier for comparison: With only three control points, the quadratic Bezier is P(t) = (1 - t)^2 P0 + 2t(1 - t) P1 + t^2 P2. At t = 0.5 the weights are 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25. For P0 = (0, 0), P1 = (2, 4) and P2 = (4, 0), the midpoint is (2, 2): exactly half the height of the middle control point. A quadratic is always a piece of a parabola, cheaper than a cubic but unable to make an S shape, which is why fonts built from quadratics need more segments.

Drawing a Bezier curve on screen: The simplest way evaluates P(t) at many values of t, say 0, 0.05, 0.1 and so on to 1, and joins the points with short straight lines using Bresenham or DDA. A smarter way uses subdivision: keep splitting the curve until each piece's control polygon is almost a straight line, then draw that line. Fonts and vector graphics renderers use these methods to turn curves into pixels.

Limitations of a single Bezier curve: The degree is tied to the number of control points: twenty points means a degree 19 polynomial, which is slow and numerically unpleasant. Control is global: moving any one control point changes the whole curve, because every Bernstein weight is non-zero for t strictly between 0 and 1. That is why long shapes are made from many cubic Bezier segments joined together. For C1 continuity at a join, the last control point of one segment, the shared end point and the first control point of the next must be collinear and equally spaced. Drawing apps enforce this when you drag a smooth node's handles.

B-splines: A B-spline curve also uses control points and blending functions, but each blending function is non-zero only over a small range of t. As a result, moving one control point changes only a few nearby segments: local control. The degree is chosen independently of the number of control points, so you can have 100 control points with a cubic curve. The joins are automatically smooth: a cubic B-spline is C2 continuous everywhere, without the designer needing to line anything up.

Knots and the uniform cubic B-spline: The parameter range is divided at values called knots. When knots are equally spaced, the B-spline is uniform. For the uniform cubic B-spline, each segment depends on just four consecutive control points, and the segment's start point is (P0 + 4 P1 + P2) / 6. For our points (0, 0), (1, 2) and (3, 3), that is x = (0 + 4 + 3)/6, about 1.17, and y = (0 + 8 + 3)/6, about 1.83. Unlike Bezier, a uniform B-spline usually does not pass through its first and last control points; repeating end knots or end points forces it to, giving a clamped B-spline.

NURBS in one paragraph: Non-uniform rational B-splines (NURBS) add non-uniform knots and a weight for each control point. The weights let NURBS represent conic sections such as circles and ellipses exactly, which ordinary polynomial curves cannot. NURBS are the standard in CAD and industrial design software, in file formats like IGES and STEP, and in 3D modelling tools for smooth surfaces.

Curves become surfaces: Applying the same idea in two parameters, u and v, gives surfaces. A bicubic Bezier patch uses a 4 x 4 grid of 16 control points. The famous Utah teapot, a standard test model of computer graphics since 1975, is made of 32 such patches. B-spline and NURBS surfaces are used for car bodies, aircraft and the smooth characters in animated films.

Real life example 1, fonts: The letters you are reading are stored as outlines made of curves, not as pixels. TrueType fonts use quadratic Bezier curves; PostScript and many OpenType fonts use cubic ones. Bangla fonts such as SolaimanLipi or Kalpurush store each juktakkhor as a set of Bezier outlines, which is why text stays sharp at any size: the curve is evaluated fresh for each size and then filled with scan-line methods.

Real life example 2, smooth motion in an app: When a Flutter or Android app animates a card sliding in, the movement often follows a cubic Bezier easing curve, such as the standard ease-in-out, defined by two inner control points. The animation feels natural because the speed rises and falls smoothly instead of starting and stopping abruptly. The same curves will reappear in the animation lesson.

Common mistakes: Saying a Bezier curve passes through all control points. Forgetting the factor 3 in the cubic's middle terms. Making arithmetic slips in de Casteljau by mixing up levels; write each level on its own line. Claiming B-splines have global control, or that Bezier curves have local control. Confusing C1 with G1.

What exams ask: Why parametric curves are used. Define C0, C1, C2 and G1 continuity. Write the Bezier equation with Bernstein polynomials and list its properties. Compute a point on a cubic Bezier curve by formula and by de Casteljau. Compare Bezier curves and B-splines, especially local control and degree. Explain knots, uniform and non-uniform B-splines and NURBS.

Recap: Parametric curves P(t) let us draw any shape smoothly. Continuity C0, C1 and C2 describes how smoothly segments join. A cubic Bezier curve uses four control points and Bernstein weights; it passes through the end points, stays inside the convex hull, and has global control. Our example gives P(0.5) = (2, 1.875) by both formula and de Casteljau. B-splines give local control, a degree independent of the number of points and automatic C2 smoothness for cubics, and NURBS add weights for exact circles. Next we put images onto surfaces: texture mapping.
key_points: Parametric curves P(t) = (x(t), y(t)) can draw loops and vertical tangents that y = f(x) cannot.
Continuity: C0 segments meet, C1 tangents match, C2 curvature matches; G1 means tangent directions match.
Cubic Bezier: P(t) = (1-t)^3 P0 + 3t(1-t)^2 P1 + 3t^2(1-t) P2 + t^3 P3, using Bernstein polynomials.
Bezier curves pass through end points, are tangent to the first and last edges, lie in the convex hull, and have global control.
de Casteljau finds P(t) by repeated linear interpolation; for (0,0), (1,2), (3,3), (4,0), P(0.5) = (2, 1.875).
For C1 joins of Bezier segments, the neighbouring control points and the shared point must be collinear and equally spaced.
B-splines give local control, a degree independent of the number of control points, and C2 continuity for cubics.
NURBS add weights and non-uniform knots, representing circles exactly; they are the CAD standard.
lessons.tip: Do de Casteljau on graph paper with a ruler at t = 0.5 for any four points. Seeing the little triangles of midpoints shrink onto the curve makes the algorithm unforgettable, and the drawing doubles as a check on your arithmetic.
lessons.task: For control points P0 = (0, 0), P1 = (0, 4), P2 = (4, 4), P3 = (4, 0), compute P(0.5) and P(0.25) of the cubic Bezier curve using de Casteljau, and check P(0.5) with the Bernstein formula. Then compute P'(0) and say which way the curve leaves P0.

quiz.q: Through which control points does a cubic Bezier curve always pass?
options: Only the first and last, P0 and P3
quiz.explain: The curve interpolates the end points and is only pulled toward the inner points.

quiz.q: For control points (0,0), (1,2), (3,3), (4,0), what is P(0.5)?
quiz.explain: Weights 1/8, 3/8, 3/8, 1/8 give x = 2 and y = 1.875; de Casteljau agrees.

quiz.q: What does C1 continuity at a join mean?
quiz.explain: C1 means equal tangent vectors at the join, so there is no corner.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of B-splines over a single Bezier curve?
options: Local control: moving one point changes only nearby segments
They always pass through every control point
quiz.explain: B-spline blending functions are non-zero only over a short range, so control is local.

quiz.q: Why can NURBS represent a circle exactly?
options: They use weights, making them rational functions
quiz.explain: Weighted, rational curves can represent conic sections exactly.

lessons.title: Texture Mapping: Texels, UV Coordinates, Filtering and Mipmaps
lessons.content:
Imagine modelling a jamdani sari, a brick wall in Puran Dhaka, or a cricket pitch, polygon by polygon, with every thread, brick and blade of grass as separate geometry. It would take millions of triangles and months of work. Instead, graphics takes a photo or a painted image and wraps it onto a few simple polygons, like printing a pattern onto fabric. This is texture mapping, introduced by Edwin Catmull in 1974. It is the single biggest reason 3D graphics went from plastic-looking shapes to believable worlds, and this lesson explains how it works, including filtering and mipmaps with worked numbers.

Texture and texel: A texture is usually a 2D image used to add surface detail. Its individual pixels are called texels, short for texture elements, to keep them separate from the pixels of the screen. Textures most often hold colour, but the same machinery can store other per-point information such as shininess, transparency or surface normals, as we will see later in the lesson.

Texture coordinates, u and v: To be independent of the image size, a texture is addressed with coordinates u and v, each from 0 to 1, across its width and height. u = 0, v = 0 is one corner and u = 1, v = 1 the opposite corner. To read a texture of width W and height H at (u, v), multiply: texel x = u W and texel y = v H. For a 256 x 256 texture, (u, v) = (0.3, 0.7) lands at texel position (76.8, 179.2), between texels, which is why we will need filtering.

Assigning texture coordinates to a mesh: The modeller gives every vertex a (u, v) pair in addition to its 3D position. A wall made of two triangles might have corners with (u, v) = (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1) and (0, 1), so the whole image covers the wall once. Setting the corners to (0, 0) to (4, 2) instead repeats the brick image four times across and twice up, provided the texture is set to wrap. For complex shapes like a character's face, artists use UV unwrapping: they cut the 3D surface along seams and flatten it onto the image, like opening a cardboard box into a flat sheet. For simple shapes there are standard projections: planar, cylindrical for a bottle or pillar, and spherical for a globe.

The mapping steps: The full process links three spaces. Texture space (u, v) is mapped onto the object's surface by the coordinates stored at its vertices. The surface is transformed and projected to screen space by the viewing pipeline. During rasterization, the inverse question is asked for every pixel: which (u, v) does this pixel see? The rasterizer interpolates u and v across the triangle, like Gouraud interpolates intensity, and then the texture is looked up at that (u, v). The texel colour is then usually combined with lighting, for example used as the diffuse colour kd in the Phong formula.

Perspective-correct interpolation: Interpolating u and v linearly in screen space is wrong under perspective. A road texture drawn that way bends and swims, because equal steps across the screen do not correspond to equal steps along the 3D surface; the far half of a triangle is squeezed on screen. The fix is to interpolate u/w, v/w and 1/w linearly, where w is the homogeneous coordinate from the perspective projection, and divide at each pixel: u = (u/w) / (1/w). Early PlayStation 1 games skipped this to save time, and their warping textures are still recognisable. All modern GPUs do it automatically.

Wrapping modes: What happens when u or v goes outside 0 to 1? With repeat, also called wrap, only the fractional part is used, so u = 2.3 reads like u = 0.3, tiling the texture; good for floors, walls and grass. With clamp, values are pinned to the edge, so the border texels stretch outward; good for decals and labels. Mirrored repeat flips every other copy so the seams match.

Texture memory in numbers: Textures are often the largest part of a game's memory. A 1024 x 1024 texture with 4 bytes per texel, for red, green, blue and alpha, takes 1024 x 1024 x 4 = 4,194,304 bytes, exactly 4 MiB, before mipmaps. A character might use separate colour, normal and specular textures of that size, 12 MiB in total. That is why games use compressed texture formats that the GPU can read directly, often cutting the size by four to eight times, and why phone games ship with smaller textures than PC games.

Magnification and minification: When the camera is close to a surface, one texel covers many screen pixels: magnification. When the surface is far away, many texels squeeze into one pixel: minification. Each causes its own problem, blocky texels when magnified and flickering, shimmering patterns when minified, and each has its own filtering solution.

Nearest-neighbour filtering: The simplest lookup rounds the texture position to the nearest texel and uses its colour. It is fast, and for pixel-art games it keeps the sharp blocky look on purpose. But in general, magnified textures look like large square tiles, and the colour jumps suddenly as you move from one texel to the next.

Bilinear filtering: Instead, take the four texels surrounding the sample position and blend them by distance, first along one direction and then the other, the same linear interpolation used everywhere in graphics. Worked example: suppose the four surrounding texel values are 10 at the top-left, 20 at the top-right, 30 at the bottom-left and 60 at the bottom-right, and the sample lies a fraction 0.25 of the way across and 0.5 of the way down. Along the top: 10 + 0.25 x (20 - 10) = 12.5. Along the bottom: 30 + 0.25 x (60 - 30) = 37.5. Then down between them: 12.5 + 0.5 x (37.5 - 12.5) = 25. The result is 25, a smooth blend, instead of the nearest texel's 10. For colour, the same is done for each of red, green and blue.

The minification problem: When a distant brick wall is drawn, a single screen pixel may cover a whole block of 8 x 8 texels, but bilinear filtering reads only 4 of them. Which 4 depends on tiny changes in camera position, so as the camera moves the pixel jumps between bright mortar and dark brick, producing shimmering, flickering and moire patterns. This is aliasing, the same problem as jagged lines in lesson 8, now inside textures.

Mipmaps: The standard cure, introduced by Lance Williams in 1983, precomputes a pyramid of smaller versions of the texture, each half the width and height of the previous: 1024 x 1024, 512 x 512, 256 x 256, down to 1 x 1. Each level is made by averaging blocks of 2 x 2 texels from the level above, so it is already pre-filtered. When drawing, the GPU estimates how many texels fall under the pixel and picks the matching level, so it always reads from a texture roughly the size of the pixel footprint. Mip comes from the Latin multum in parvo, much in a small space.

The cost of mipmaps: Each level has a quarter of the texels of the one above, so the total memory is 1 + 1/4 + 1/16 + ... times the original, which approaches 4/3. Mipmaps therefore cost only about one third extra memory, and they also speed up rendering, because reading from small textures uses the memory cache much better. For a 1024 x 1024 texture, the full chain has 11 levels.

Trilinear and anisotropic filtering: When the right size falls between two mip levels, trilinear filtering does a bilinear lookup in each of the two nearest levels and blends the results, removing visible lines where the level changes. A surface seen at a steep angle, like a long road stretching away, is squeezed much more in one direction than the other; anisotropic filtering takes several samples along the long direction so the road stays sharp in the distance. The 4x, 8x or 16x settings in a game's options menu are exactly this.

Beyond colour: bump mapping and normal mapping: James Blinn showed in 1978 that small surface detail can be faked by perturbing the normal used in lighting, without changing geometry. A bump map stores heights; the renderer computes how the surface would tilt and adjusts N. A normal map stores the perturbed normal directly, as RGB values encoding x, y and z, which is why normal maps look bluish purple. Since the Phong illumination model reacts to N, a flat wall suddenly shows lit and shadowed edges on every brick. The silhouette stays flat, though; displacement mapping actually moves vertices when real geometry is needed.

Other maps in brief: Specular maps say which parts of a surface are shiny, for example wet patches on a road. Alpha maps make parts transparent, like the gaps between leaves on a tree drawn as a single rectangle. Environment maps store the surroundings as an image, often a cube of six faces, and are looked up by the reflection direction R to fake mirror-like reflections on cars and water. Light maps store precomputed lighting for static scenes.

Real life example 1, a cricket game: The pitch, outfield and crowd are mostly textures on simple geometry. The pitch uses a repeating grass texture blended with a worn-patch texture, mipmapped so the far end does not shimmer, with anisotropic filtering because the pitch is viewed at a low angle. Player shirts carry team logos through UV-mapped textures, and a normal map adds fabric folds without extra triangles.

Real life example 2, a heritage walkthrough: A virtual tour of Lalbagh Fort scans the walls with photographs and maps them onto a simplified 3D model. Each brick and stain is real, from the photos, but the model has only a few thousand triangles, so it runs smoothly on a phone. Normal maps restore the feel of the rough brick surface under moving virtual light.

Common mistakes: Confusing texels with pixels. Forgetting that u and v run from 0 to 1, independent of the image size. Thinking bilinear filtering solves minification aliasing; mipmaps do. Thinking normal mapping changes the outline. Forgetting the perspective-correct division, or not knowing why it is needed.

What exams ask: Define texture mapping and texels, and explain the mapping from texture space to object space to screen space. Explain how texture coordinates are assigned and interpolated, and why perspective correction is needed. Compare nearest and bilinear filtering with a numeric example. Explain mipmapping, its memory cost and trilinear filtering. Explain bump mapping and environment mapping.

Recap: Texture mapping wraps images onto surfaces using (u, v) coordinates at vertices, interpolated in a perspective-correct way during rasterization. Nearest filtering picks one texel; bilinear blends four, giving 25 in our example. Mipmaps store prefiltered half-size levels for distant surfaces at about one third extra memory, with trilinear and anisotropic filtering refining the result. Bump and normal maps fake detail by changing normals, and environment maps fake reflections. Next we see how GPUs run this entire pipeline in hardware with programmable shaders.
key_points: Texture mapping wraps an image onto surfaces; its elements are texels, addressed by u and v from 0 to 1.
Each vertex stores (u, v); the rasterizer interpolates them and looks up the texture for every pixel.
Perspective-correct interpolation interpolates u/w, v/w and 1/w and divides per pixel to avoid warping.
Repeat (wrap) tiles a texture; clamp stretches the edge texels.
Nearest filtering picks one texel; bilinear blends the four nearest, for example 10, 20, 30, 60 at (0.25, 0.5) gives 25.
Minification causes shimmering aliasing; mipmaps store halved, prefiltered levels for about 1/3 extra memory.
Trilinear filtering blends two mip levels; anisotropic filtering samples along the stretched direction.
Bump and normal mapping fake surface detail by perturbing normals; environment maps fake reflections.
lessons.tip: Open any game or 3D app that lets you change texture filtering and anisotropic settings, and look at a long road or floor while switching them. Seeing shimmer appear and disappear explains mipmaps and anisotropy faster than any diagram.
lessons.task: Four texels around a sample have values 40 (top-left), 80 (top-right), 20 (bottom-left) and 100 (bottom-right). Compute the bilinear result at fractions 0.5 across and 0.25 down, and compare it with nearest-neighbour. Then list the mip level sizes of a 512 x 512 texture and compute the total memory as a fraction of the original.

quiz.q: What is a texel?
options: An individual element of a texture image
quiz.explain: Texels are the pixels of the texture, named separately from screen pixels.

quiz.q: Bilinear filtering of texels 10, 20 (top) and 30, 60 (bottom) at 0.25 across and 0.5 down gives:
quiz.explain: Top 12.5, bottom 37.5, halfway between them is 25.

quiz.q: About how much extra memory does a full mipmap chain need?
quiz.explain: 1 + 1/4 + 1/16 + ... approaches 4/3 of the original.

quiz.q: Why is perspective-correct texture interpolation needed?
options: Linear interpolation in screen space distorts textures under perspective
quiz.explain: Equal screen steps are not equal surface steps, so u/w, v/w and 1/w are interpolated instead.

quiz.q: What does normal mapping change?
options: The normals used in lighting, faking surface detail
quiz.explain: Only the shading normals change; geometry and outline stay the same.

lessons.title: The GPU Rendering Pipeline and Shaders
lessons.content:
Every algorithm in this course so far, transformations, clipping, projection, scan conversion, the z-buffer, lighting, shading and texture mapping, has to run for millions of vertices and pixels, sixty or more times every second, when you play a game or scroll a map on your phone. A normal CPU, with a handful of powerful cores, cannot keep up. The graphics processing unit, or GPU, is a chip built for exactly this job: thousands of small cores running the same short program on many vertices or pixels at once. This lesson ties the whole course together by walking through the modern GPU pipeline and the small programs, called shaders, that we write to control it.

Why a GPU: The work in graphics is massively parallel. The lighting of one pixel does not depend on the lighting of its neighbour, and transforming one vertex does not depend on the next. A 1920 x 1080 screen has 2,073,600 pixels; at 60 frames per second that is about 124 million pixel computations per second even if each pixel is shaded only once. A GPU, with thousands of simple cores and very fast memory, performs these in parallel. The same parallel power is why GPUs are now also used for machine learning.

Graphics APIs: Programs do not talk to the GPU hardware directly. They use an application programming interface: OpenGL and its mobile version OpenGL ES, Vulkan, Microsoft's Direct3D, Apple's Metal, and WebGL in browsers. The API lets the program upload vertex data and textures, set the matrices, choose shader programs and issue draw calls. Flutter, which this app itself is built with, draws its interface through a GPU renderer, so even flat 2D buttons go through the same pipeline.

The pipeline at a glance: The modern pipeline has these stages: input assembly, which gathers vertices into triangles; the vertex shader, programmable, run once per vertex; optional tessellation and geometry shaders; primitive assembly, clipping and the perspective divide; viewport transform; rasterization, which turns each triangle into fragments; the fragment shader, programmable, run once per fragment; and per-fragment operations, the depth test, stencil test and blending, writing to the frame buffer. Every stage corresponds to a lesson you have already done.

Fixed-function versus programmable: Early GPUs, up to about 2001, had a fixed-function pipeline: the transformation and lighting steps were built in, and programmers could only switch features on and off and set parameters, such as choosing Gouraud lighting with given light positions. Then programmable shaders arrived, letting developers write their own code for the vertex and fragment stages. Since around 2008 in desktop OpenGL and with OpenGL ES 2.0 on phones, shaders are not optional: every draw call needs a vertex and a fragment shader.

Uniforms, attributes and varyings: Shaders receive three kinds of data. Attributes are per-vertex inputs read from vertex buffers, such as position, normal and texture coordinates. Uniforms are values the CPU sets once for a whole draw call, such as the matrices, the light position and the texture to use; every vertex and fragment sees the same value. Varyings, written as out in the vertex shader and in in the fragment shader, are the values handed from one stage to the next and interpolated by the rasterizer in between. Knowing which data belongs to which kind is half of writing shaders.

The vertex shader: It runs once for every vertex. Its main job is to transform the vertex position from model space to clip space using the combined projection, view and model matrices from lesson 17, and write the result to a built-in output, gl_Position in OpenGL's GLSL language. It also passes per-vertex data onward, such as the normal transformed to world or eye space, texture coordinates and colours. A vertex shader cannot create or delete vertices and does not know about its neighbours: one vertex in, one vertex out.

A tiny vertex shader in GLSL, described line by line: It declares inputs, in vec3 position and in vec3 normal and in vec2 uv; uniforms, values constant for the whole draw call, uniform mat4 model, view and projection; and outputs, out vec3 vNormal and out vec2 vUV. Its main function sets gl_Position = projection * view * model * vec4(position, 1.0), sets vNormal = mat3(model) * normal, and sets vUV = uv. Note the vec4 with w = 1.0: the homogeneous coordinate from lesson 9. Strictly, normals should be transformed by the inverse transpose of the model matrix when it contains non-uniform scaling; for rotations and uniform scaling mat3(model) works.

Clipping, divide and viewport: After the vertex shader, the fixed hardware assembles triangles, clips them against the view volume in clip coordinates, exactly the -w to w tests of lesson 17 using the polygon clipping ideas of lesson 14, divides by w to get normalized device coordinates, and applies the viewport transform to get pixel positions. Triangles facing away can be removed here by back-face culling, the N . V test of lesson 18 done using the winding order of the projected vertices.

Rasterization: The rasterizer finds which pixel centres each triangle covers, a parallel version of scan conversion. For each covered pixel it generates a fragment, a candidate pixel carrying a position, a depth, and the vertex shader's outputs interpolated across the triangle in the perspective-correct way of lesson 23. This interpolation is where Gouraud's idea lives on: every value the vertex shader outputs is smoothly blended across the triangle for free.

The fragment shader: It runs once for every fragment and computes its colour. This is where per-pixel lighting, texturing and special effects happen. A Phong fragment shader in words: normalise the interpolated normal, since interpolation shortens it; compute L and V; compute diffuse = max(dot(N, L), 0.0); compute R = reflect(-L, N) and specular = pow(max(dot(R, V), 0.0), shininess); sample the texture with texture(albedo, vUV); and output colour = texColour * (ambient + diffuse) + specular. That is the illumination model of lesson 20 with the Phong shading of lesson 21, running on every pixel.

Why the GPU is fast at this: A GPU groups fragments, typically 32 or 64 at a time, and runs the same instruction on all of them together, a style called single instruction, multiple threads. Neighbouring fragments of one triangle run the same shader, so this works well. Branches, such as an if statement where some fragments go one way and others the other, force the group to run both paths, so shader programmers avoid heavy branching. GPUs also hide slow memory reads by switching to another group while one waits for its texture data.

Per-fragment operations: The finished fragment still has to pass tests before reaching the frame buffer. The depth test compares its depth with the depth buffer, the z-buffer of lesson 18, and discards it if something nearer is already there. The stencil test checks a mask, used for mirrors, portals and outlines. Finally, blending combines the fragment's colour with the colour already stored, for transparency: result = alpha x source + (1 - alpha) x destination. For a red glass with alpha 0.25 over a white background, red channel = 0.25 x 1 + 0.75 x 1 = 1, and green = 0.25 x 0 + 0.75 x 1 = 0.75, giving a pale pink (1, 0.75, 0.75).

Why transparent objects are drawn last: Blending depends on what is already in the frame buffer, so order matters, unlike the depth test. Engines therefore draw all opaque objects first with depth testing and depth writing on, then draw transparent objects sorted from back to front, the painter's algorithm, usually with depth writing off. This is the hybrid we mentioned in lesson 18.

Double buffering and frame rate: The GPU draws into a hidden back buffer while the screen shows the front buffer; when the frame is complete, they are swapped, so the viewer never sees a half-drawn image. Waiting for the display's refresh before swapping, called vsync, prevents tearing, where the top and bottom of the screen show different frames. At 60 Hz each frame has about 16.7 milliseconds; at 120 Hz, about 8.3. If the work takes longer, frames are dropped and motion stutters.

Other shader stages in brief: Tessellation shaders subdivide patches into many triangles on the GPU, for example turning a coarse Bezier surface from lesson 22 into a smooth mesh close to the camera and a coarse one far away. Geometry shaders can emit new primitives per input primitive, though they are often slow. Compute shaders run general calculations on the GPU outside the drawing pipeline, used for physics, particles, image processing and machine learning.

Performance basics: The CPU sends work to the GPU through draw calls, each with some overhead, so engines batch many objects into fewer calls and use instancing to draw many copies of one mesh, like a thousand trees, in a single call. Overdraw, shading the same pixel many times because of overlapping surfaces, wastes fragment shader work; drawing opaque objects roughly front to back lets the depth test reject hidden fragments early. Texture size and mipmaps matter for memory bandwidth, as we saw last lesson.

Real life example 1, a phone game frame: In one frame of a popular battle game on a phone, the CPU decides what is visible and issues a few hundred draw calls. The vertex shader transforms tens of thousands of vertices of characters and terrain; the rasterizer generates millions of fragments; fragment shaders sample textures and compute lighting; the depth buffer resolves visibility; and smoke and glass are blended at the end. All of it fits in 16.7 milliseconds, sixty times a second.

Real life example 2, a photo filter in an app: When a camera app in Bangladesh applies a beauty filter live, it draws the camera image as a texture on a single rectangle covering the screen. A fragment shader runs for every pixel, blurring skin, adjusting colour in an HSV-like space and brightening, all in parallel on the GPU, which is why the filter runs in real time even on a mid-range phone.

Common mistakes: Thinking the vertex shader colours pixels; it processes vertices. Thinking the fragment shader can move a pixel to a different position; it cannot. Forgetting to normalise interpolated normals in the fragment shader. Drawing transparent objects in random order. Writing matrix multiplication in the wrong order: projection * view * model * position.

What exams ask: Draw and explain the stages of the modern graphics pipeline, marking programmable and fixed stages. Compare fixed-function and programmable pipelines. Explain the roles of vertex and fragment shaders with a simple example. Explain rasterization and fragments. Explain the depth test, blending and double buffering. Explain why GPUs suit graphics.

Recap: The GPU runs the graphics pipeline in parallel. The vertex shader transforms each vertex with projection times view times model and passes data on; fixed hardware clips, divides by w, maps to the viewport and rasterizes triangles into fragments with interpolated values; the fragment shader computes each fragment's colour with lighting and textures; then the depth test, stencil test and blending write the frame buffer, with double buffering and vsync for smooth display. Every earlier lesson is one stage of this pipeline. The last lesson covers animation basics and ray tracing.
key_points: GPUs have thousands of simple cores that process vertices and pixels in parallel; a 1080p screen at 60 fps needs about 124 million pixel computations per second.
Programs use APIs such as OpenGL, OpenGL ES, Vulkan, Direct3D, Metal and WebGL.
Pipeline: input assembly, vertex shader, clipping and divide, viewport, rasterization, fragment shader, depth/stencil test and blending.
The vertex shader runs per vertex, computes gl_Position = projection * view * model * vec4(position, 1.0), and passes data on.
The rasterizer creates fragments and interpolates vertex outputs across each triangle, perspective-correct.
The fragment shader runs per fragment and computes colour with lighting and texture lookups.
Blending: result = alpha x source + (1 - alpha) x destination; opaque objects first, transparent ones back to front.
Double buffering swaps a hidden back buffer with the front buffer; vsync prevents tearing; 60 Hz gives about 16.7 ms per frame.
lessons.tip: Take the pipeline diagram and, next to each stage, write the number of the lesson in this course that explains it. If you can fill every box, you have the whole course in one picture for revision.
lessons.task: Write in plain words what a vertex shader and a fragment shader would do to draw a textured, lit rotating cube. Then compute the blended colour of a blue glass (0, 0, 1) with alpha 0.4 drawn over a yellow wall (1, 1, 0).

quiz.q: How often does a vertex shader run?
quiz.explain: The vertex shader processes each vertex independently.

quiz.q: What is the correct GLSL order for computing gl_Position?
quiz.explain: With column vectors, the model matrix applies first, so it is written next to the position.

quiz.q: Which pipeline stage turns triangles into fragments?
quiz.explain: The rasterizer finds covered pixels and creates fragments with interpolated values.

quiz.q: A red glass (1, 0, 0) with alpha 0.25 is blended over white (1, 1, 1). What is the result?
quiz.explain: Each channel is 0.25 x source + 0.75 x 1, giving (1, 0.75, 0.75).

quiz.q: Why is double buffering used?
options: So the viewer never sees a half-drawn frame
quiz.explain: Drawing happens in a hidden back buffer that is swapped in only when complete.

lessons.title: Animation Basics and an Introduction to Ray Tracing
lessons.content:
Think of a flip book: a stack of small drawings, each slightly different, which seem to move when you flick through them quickly. Every cartoon on television, every Meena episode, every game and every app animation works the same way. And think of the photo-realistic films where you cannot tell a computer-made car from a real one: much of that realism comes from a method that follows rays of light, called ray tracing. This final lesson covers both topics: the basics of computer animation, with keyframes, interpolation and easing worked in numbers, and an introduction to ray tracing, with a worked ray-sphere intersection. It ends by tying the whole course together.

What animation is: Animation is a sequence of still images, frames, shown fast enough that the eye and brain perceive continuous motion. Film traditionally uses 24 frames per second; television and video use 25 or 30; games aim for 30, 60 or more, because players interact and smoother motion feels more responsive. A 2-second animation at 30 frames per second therefore needs 60 frames. Below about 12 frames per second, motion looks jerky.

Traditional animation and its ideas: Hand-drawn studios had senior animators draw the important poses, called keyframes, and assistants draw the frames between them, called in-betweens. Disney's animators summarised what makes motion feel alive in the twelve principles of animation, such as squash and stretch, anticipation, slow in and slow out, and arcs. Computer animation borrows the same vocabulary: the computer now does the in-betweening.

Keyframe animation on a computer: The animator sets values of some properties, such as position, rotation, scale or colour, at chosen times. The software computes the values for every frame in between by interpolation. Worked example: a ball has x = 100 at time 0 seconds and x = 400 at time 2 seconds. At time 0.5 seconds, the fraction of the way through is s = 0.5 / 2 = 0.25. Linear interpolation gives x = 100 + 0.25 x (400 - 100) = 175. At 30 frames per second, frame 15 shows the ball at 175.

Easing: Linear interpolation moves at constant speed and starts and stops abruptly, which looks mechanical. Real objects speed up and slow down: slow in and slow out. Easing functions reshape the fraction s before interpolating. A common one is smoothstep, e(s) = 3s^2 - 2s^3, which starts and ends with zero speed. At s = 0.25, e = 3 x 0.0625 - 2 x 0.015625 = 0.15625, so x = 100 + 0.15625 x 300, about 146.9 instead of 175: the ball is still gathering speed. Easing curves in animation tools are usually cubic Bezier curves, the same curves from lesson 22, which is why app frameworks describe easing with four numbers, the two inner control points.

Interpolating along paths and rotations: When an object should follow a curved path, the keyframe positions are joined with splines such as Catmull-Rom or B-splines instead of straight lines, so motion flows smoothly through each key. Rotations are trickier: interpolating rotation angles separately can give strange wobbles and a problem called gimbal lock, so animation systems often store rotations as quaternions and interpolate them with spherical linear interpolation, known as slerp. You only need the names for most exams.

Other animation techniques: Morphing gradually changes one shape into another by interpolating corresponding points, as in face-changing effects. Procedural animation computes motion from rules, such as waves on water or a flag in the wind. Physically based animation simulates forces: gravity, collisions and springs, used for falling objects, cloth and hair. Skeletal animation gives a character an internal skeleton of bones; animators move the bones, and each vertex of the skin follows a weighted mix of nearby bones, called skinning. Motion capture records the movement of real actors with markers or cameras and applies it to a skeleton, which is how many game characters move so naturally.

Why ray tracing: The rasterization pipeline of the last lesson projects triangles onto the screen and asks which pixels each one covers. It is fast, but effects that involve light bouncing between objects, such as true reflections, refractions through glass and accurate shadows, need extra tricks like environment maps and shadow maps. Ray tracing turns the question around: for each pixel, which object does the light come from? It follows rays through the scene, so reflections, refraction and shadows come out naturally.

The basic ray tracing algorithm: For every pixel, cast a primary ray from the eye through the pixel's position on the image plane. Find the nearest object the ray hits, solving visibility like a z-buffer does. At the hit point, compute the colour with an illumination model such as Phong. For shadows, cast a shadow ray from the hit point toward each light: if it hits something first, that light is blocked. For shiny surfaces, cast a reflected ray in the mirror direction R and add its colour; for transparent ones, cast a refracted ray using Snell's law. These secondary rays recurse, up to a fixed depth. This is Whitted-style ray tracing, from Turner Whitted's 1980 paper.

A ray as an equation: A ray starts at an origin O and travels in a unit direction D: P(t) = O + t D, for t >= 0. Larger t means farther along the ray. To find where the ray hits an object, substitute P(t) into the object's equation and solve for t. The smallest positive t is the nearest hit.

Ray-sphere intersection: A sphere with centre C and radius r contains the points with |P - C|^2 = r^2. Substituting the ray gives a quadratic equation: t^2 + b t + c = 0, with b = 2 D . (O - C) and c = |O - C|^2 - r^2, when D is a unit vector. The discriminant b^2 - 4c decides everything: negative, the ray misses; zero, it just touches; positive, it enters and leaves at two values of t.

Ray-sphere worked: Eye at O = (0, 0, 0), looking along D = (0, 0, -1); a sphere at C = (0, 0, -10) with r = 3. Then O - C = (0, 0, 10), b = 2 x (-1 x 10) = -20, and c = 100 - 9 = 91. The discriminant is 400 - 364 = 36, whose square root is 6. So t = (20 - 6) / 2 = 7 and t = (20 + 6) / 2 = 13. The nearest hit is at t = 7: the point (0, 0, -7), the front of the sphere, while t = 13 is where the ray would leave the back. The normal at the hit is (P - C) / r = (0, 0, 3) / 3 = (0, 0, 1), pointing back at the viewer, ready for lighting. A ray with D = (0, 0.6, -0.8) gives b = -16 and discriminant 256 - 364 = -108, negative: it passes above the sphere and misses.

The cost and its cures: A naive ray tracer tests every ray against every object, and a 1920 x 1080 image has 2,073,600 primary rays before counting shadows and reflections. Real ray tracers organise objects in acceleration structures, most commonly a bounding volume hierarchy, a tree of boxes, so each ray tests only a few objects, cutting the work from linear to roughly logarithmic in the number of objects. Antialiasing is done by casting several rays per pixel and averaging them.

Beyond Whitted ray tracing: Whitted ray tracing gives sharp shadows and perfect mirrors, but no soft shadows or light bouncing between matte surfaces. Distributed ray tracing sends many rays with small random variations to get soft shadows, blurry reflections, depth of field and motion blur. Path tracing goes further, following random bounce paths to simulate all light transport, solving what is called the rendering equation, and is the standard method for film. Radiosity is an older method for light bouncing between diffuse surfaces in architecture.

Rasterization versus ray tracing: Rasterization loops over objects and asks which pixels each covers; it is extremely fast and is what GPUs have been built for, but global effects need tricks. Ray tracing loops over pixels and asks which object each sees; it handles reflection, refraction and shadows naturally but costs far more. Since 2018, consumer GPUs include hardware ray tracing cores, and modern games combine both: rasterize the main image, then trace a limited number of rays for reflections, shadows and lighting. Animated films use path tracing on render farms, taking minutes to hours per frame.

Real life example 1, an animated short: A student animation team in Dhaka making a short film about a rickshaw ride sets keyframes for the rickshaw's position every second, eases the starts and stops, uses a skeleton for the rickshaw puller, and renders the final frames with a path tracer overnight on several computers. At 24 frames per second, a 3-minute film needs 4,320 frames.

Real life example 2, a game with ray-traced reflections: In a modern racing game on a powerful PC, the main image is rasterized as in lesson 24, but the reflections of street lights in wet roads and in car paint are produced by tracing rays on the GPU's ray tracing cores. Turning that setting off falls back to the environment maps of lesson 23, which look good but miss nearby moving cars.

The whole course in one paragraph: Pixels live in a frame buffer; lines, circles and polygons are rasterized by DDA, Bresenham, midpoint and scan-line algorithms; matrices in homogeneous coordinates move objects; windows, viewports and clipping decide what is shown; 3D transforms, projection and the viewing pipeline turn a scene into a picture; hidden surface removal keeps the nearest surfaces; colour models, illumination and shading give realistic colour and light; curves and textures add smooth shapes and detail; the GPU runs it all with shaders; and animation and ray tracing bring motion and realism.

Common mistakes: Confusing keyframes with in-betweens. Forgetting to convert time into a fraction before interpolating. Taking the larger root of the ray-sphere equation instead of the smallest positive one. Forgetting that a negative discriminant means a miss. Thinking ray tracing and rasterization cannot be combined.

What exams ask: Define animation, frame rate, keyframes and in-betweening, and compute an interpolated value. Explain easing and morphing. Describe the ray tracing algorithm with primary, shadow, reflected and refracted rays. Derive and solve ray-sphere intersection. Compare ray tracing with rasterization.

Recap: Animation shows frames fast enough to look continuous; keyframes are interpolated, with easing such as smoothstep for natural motion, giving 146.9 instead of 175 in our example. Ray tracing casts rays from the eye through each pixel, finds the nearest hit, and recursively casts shadow, reflection and refraction rays; our ray meets the sphere at t = 7. Rasterization is fast and ray tracing is realistic, and modern systems combine both. That completes Computer Graphics: from a single pixel to a photo-realistic, animated world.
